arXiv:2603.00195v1 [cs.CR] 27 Feb 2026

Formal Analysis and Supply Chain Security
for Agentic AI Skills

Varun Pratap Bhardwaj email: varun.pratap.bhardwaj@gmail.com Affiliation: Independent Research, Solution Architect, India
Abstract.

The rapid proliferation of agentic AI skill ecosystems—exemplified by OpenClaw (228,000 GitHub stars) and Anthropic Agent Skills (75,600 stars)—has introduced a critical supply chain attack surface. The ClawHavoc campaign (January–February 2026) infiltrated over 1,200 malicious skills into the OpenClaw marketplace, while MalTool catalogued 6,487 malicious tools that evade conventional detection. In response, twelve reactive security tools emerged, yet all rely on heuristic methods that provide no formal guarantees. We present SkillFortify, the first formal analysis framework for agent skill supply chains, with six contributions: (1) the DY-Skill attacker model, a Dolev–Yao adaptation to the five-phase skill lifecycle with a maximality proof; (2) a sound static analysis framework grounded in abstract interpretation; (3) capability-based sandboxing with a confinement proof; (4) an Agent Dependency Graph with SAT-based resolution and lockfile semantics; (5) a trust score algebra with formal monotonicity; and (6) SkillFortifyBench, a 540-skill benchmark. SkillFortify achieves 96.95% F1 (95% CI: [95.1%, 98.4%]) with 100% precision and 0% false positive rate on 540 skills, while SAT-based resolution handles 1,000-node graphs in under 100 ms.

Keywords: 
supply chain security, agent skills, formal analysis, capability-based security, abstract interpretation, Dolev–Yao model, AI safety

1. Introduction

On January 27, 2026, security researchers at Ethiack disclosed CVE-2026-25253 (Ethiack, 2026), a remote code execution vulnerability in the OpenClaw agent skill runtime—the first Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier assigned to an agentic AI system. Within days, the ClawHavoc campaign (Zhang et al., 2026) exploited this and related weaknesses to infiltrate over 1,200 malicious skills into the OpenClaw marketplace, deploying the AMOS credential stealer to developer workstations. Concurrently, MalTool benchmarked 6,487 malicious tools targeting LLM-based agents (Wang et al., 2026b), demonstrating that VirusTotal fails to detect the majority of agent-targeted malware. A large-scale empirical analysis of 42,447 agent skills found that 26.1% exhibit at least one security vulnerability (Park et al., 2026).

These incidents are not isolated. They reflect a structural vulnerability in the emerging agent skill ecosystem: developers install and execute third-party skills with implicit trust and no formal analysis. The agent skill supply chain—spanning authorship, registry publication, developer installation, runtime execution, and state persistence—reproduces the trust pathologies of traditional package ecosystems (npm, PyPI, crates.io) but with amplified risk, because agent skills execute with broad system privileges in the context of a powerful language model.

1.1. The Defense Gap

The security community responded rapidly. Within thirty days of the ClawHavoc disclosure, twelve reactive security tools appeared on GitHub (Zhang et al., 2026). The most prominent include:

  • •

    Snyk agent-scan (∼{\sim}1,500 stars): Acquired Invariant Labs and applies LLM-as-judge combined with heuristic rules to scan agent configurations (Snyk, 2026).

  • •

    Cisco skill-scanner (994 stars): Employs YARA pattern matching and signature-based detection for known malicious skill patterns (Cisco, 2026).

  • •

    ToolShield (Wang et al., 2026a): A heuristic defense achieving a 30% reduction in attack success rate through behavioral heuristics.

Despite their utility, every existing tool shares a fundamental limitation: they are heuristic. They detect known patterns but cannot prove the absence of malicious behavior. Cisco’s own documentation for their skill-scanner states explicitly: “no findings does not mean no risk” (Cisco, 2026). The closest academic work toward formal guarantees is a four-page ICSE-NIER vision paper proposing Alloy-based modeling of tool safety (Nguyen et al., 2026), which provides neither an implementation nor empirical evaluation.

This gap is the central problem we address: the agent skill ecosystem has attack frameworks but no defense frameworks with formal guarantees.

1.2. Our Approach

We present SkillFortify, the first formal analysis framework for agent skill supply chains. SkillFortify provides sound static analysis with mathematical guarantees—not heuristic scanning—that skills cannot exceed their declared capabilities. Where existing tools answer “did we detect a known bad pattern?”, SkillFortify answers “can this skill access resources beyond what it declares?” and provides a machine-checkable certificate when the answer is no.

Our approach draws on four decades of formal methods research, adapting established foundations to the novel domain of agent skill security: the Dolev–Yao attacker model (Dolev and Yao, 1983) for supply chain threat modeling, abstract interpretation (Cousot and Cousot, 1977) for sound static analysis, capability-based security (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966; Miller, 2006) for sandboxing, and SAT-based dependency resolution (Tucker et al., 2007) for supply chain management.

1.3. Contributions

This paper makes six contributions:

  1. (1)

    DY-Skill attacker model (Section 3). We introduce a novel adaptation of the Dolev–Yao formalism (Dolev and Yao, 1983) to the five-phase agent skill supply chain. The DY-Skill attacker can intercept, inject, synthesize, decompose, and replay skill messages. We prove that this attacker is maximal: any symbolic attacker on the supply chain can be simulated by a DY-Skill trace (Theorem 3.6).

  2. (2)

    Static analysis with soundness guarantees (Section 4). We develop a three-phase static analysis framework grounded in abstract interpretation over a four-element capability lattice ({𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤,𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭},⊑)(\{\mathsf{NONE},\mathsf{READ},\mathsf{WRITE},\mathsf{ADMIN}\},\sqsubseteq). We prove that if our analysis reports a skill as safe, then its concrete execution cannot access resources beyond its declared capabilities (Theorem 4.9).

  3. (3)

    Capability-based sandboxing with confinement proof (Section 5). We formalize a capability model for agent skills based on the object-capability discipline (Miller, 2006; Maffeis et al., 2010). We prove that in a capability-safe execution environment, no skill can acquire authority exceeding the transitive closure of its declared capability set—the no authority amplification property (Theorem 5.6).

  4. (4)

    Agent Dependency Graph with SAT-based resolution (Section 6). We define the Agent Dependency Graph 𝒢=(𝒮,V,D,C,𝖢𝖺𝗉)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{S},V,D,C,\mathsf{Cap}) extending classical package dependency models (Mancinelli et al., 2006; Tucker et al., 2007) with per-skill capability constraints. We encode the resolution problem as a SAT instance with security bounds and prove that any satisfying assignment corresponds to a secure installation with a deterministic lockfile (Theorem 6.10).

  5. (5)

    Trust score algebra with formal propagation (Section 7). We introduce a multi-signal trust scoring system with provenance, behavioral, community, and historical dimensions. Trust propagates multiplicatively through dependency chains and decays exponentially for unmaintained skills. We prove the monotonicity property: additional positive evidence never reduces a skill’s trust score (Theorem 7.12).

  6. (6)

    SkillFortifyBench and empirical evaluation (Section 9). We construct SkillFortifyBench, a 540-skill benchmark comprising 270 malicious and 270 benign skills drawn from MalTool (Wang et al., 2026b), ClawHavoc (Zhang et al., 2026), and curated clean sources. SkillFortify achieves an F1 score of 96.95% with 100% precision and 0% false positive rate on benign skills. SAT-based dependency resolution handles 1,000-node graphs in under 100 ms. We evaluate on SkillFortifyBench (540 skills) and position our results against reported metrics from existing tools, demonstrating that combined pattern matching and information flow analysis detects attack patterns invisible to pure pattern matching alone.

1.4. Paper Organization

Section 2 surveys the agent skill ecosystem, attack landscape, existing defenses, and formal methods foundations. Section 3 presents the DY-Skill attacker model and threat taxonomy. Section 4 develops the static analysis framework. Section 5 formalizes capability-based sandboxing. Section 6 defines the Agent Dependency Graph and lockfile semantics. Section 7 introduces the trust score algebra. Section 8 describes the SkillFortify implementation. Section 9 presents the empirical evaluation. Section 10 positions our contributions against related work. Section 11 discusses limitations and future directions, and Section 12 concludes. Full proofs appear in Appendix A, benchmark details in Appendix B, and the lockfile schema in Appendix C.

2. Background

This section surveys the agent skill ecosystem (§2.1), the attack landscape (§2.2), existing defense tools (§2.3), traditional supply chain security foundations (§2.4), and the formal methods we build upon (§2.5). A dedicated comparison with related work appears in Section 10.

2.1. Agent Skill Ecosystems

The year 2025–2026 witnessed explosive growth in agent skill platforms. An agent skill is a third-party extension—typically a code module, configuration file, or API endpoint—that augments an LLM-based agent with domain-specific capabilities such as web search, file manipulation, database querying, or interaction with external services.

Three ecosystems dominate the landscape:

OpenClaw.

With 228,000 GitHub stars as of February 2026, OpenClaw is the largest open-source agent framework. Its marketplace operates on an install-and-run trust model: developers discover skills through a web interface or CLI, install them with a single command, and skills execute with the agent’s full system privileges. No formal review, signing, or capability declaration is required for publication.

Anthropic Agent Skills.

Anthropic’s official skill repository (75,600 stars) provides curated skills for Claude Code and Claude Desktop. Skills are defined as YAML/Markdown files in .claude/skills/ directories and may include shell commands, code blocks, and instructions. While Anthropic maintains a moderation pipeline, no formal capability model constrains skill behavior at runtime.

Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2025) standardizes how agents interact with external data sources and tools through JSON-RPC servers. MCP servers declare tool schemas (input/output types) but not capability requirements—a server that claims to “search files” may also execute arbitrary shell commands, and the protocol provides no mechanism to detect or prevent this.

All three ecosystems share a common structural weakness: the absence of a formal capability model that constrains what a skill can do to what it declares. This is the gap our work fills.

2.2. Attack Landscape

Five incidents and studies define the attack landscape as of February 2026. Early work on LLM platform plugin security (Hou et al., 2023) identified many of the attack vectors that have since materialized at scale, and recent systematic analyses of the Model Context Protocol (He et al., 2025) confirm that these vulnerabilities persist in modern agent architectures:

CVE-2026-25253 (January 27, 2026).

The first CVE assigned to an agentic AI system. Ethiack demonstrated remote code execution in the OpenClaw skill runtime through a crafted skill package. The proof-of-concept repository received 75 stars within days (Ethiack, 2026).

ClawHavoc Campaign (Late January–Early February 2026).

A coordinated supply chain attack documented in the “SoK: Agentic Skills in the Wild” systematization (Zhang et al., 2026). Attackers published over 1,200 malicious skills to the OpenClaw marketplace, deploying the AMOS credential stealer. The paper identifies seven distinct skill design patterns exploited by the campaign and categorizes the full attack lifecycle.

MalTool (February 12, 2026).

Researchers from Dawn Song’s group catalogued 6,487 malicious tools targeting LLM-based agents (Wang et al., 2026b). Their benchmark demonstrated that VirusTotal—the de facto standard for malware detection—fails to identify the majority of agent-targeted malware, underscoring the inadequacy of signature-based approaches for this domain. Complementary MCP-specific attack research—MCP-ITP (Liu et al., 2026) (automated implicit tool poisoning) and MCPTox (Pasquini et al., 2025) (benchmarking tool poisoning on real-world MCP servers)—demonstrates that protocol-level vulnerabilities compound the skill-level threat.

Agent Skills in the Wild (January 2026).

A large-scale empirical study scanned 42,447 agent skills across multiple registries (Park et al., 2026). Key findings: 26.1% of skills exhibit at least one security vulnerability, 14 distinct vulnerability patterns were identified, and their SkillScan tool achieves 86.7% precision—leaving a 13.3% gap that formal methods can address.

Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild (February 2026).

A large-scale registry scan covering 98,380 skills across multiple agent platforms identified 157 confirmed malicious entries (Li et al., 2026), independently corroborating the vulnerability rates reported by Park et al. (Park et al., 2026) on a substantially larger corpus.

Multi-agent data leakage.

OMNI-LEAK (Cohen et al., 2026) demonstrates that multi-agent architectures create implicit information channels through which sensitive data can leak across trust boundaries—even when individual agents appear well-isolated. This motivates our information flow analysis component (Section 4).

Agent reliability.

Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2026) provide empirical evidence that LLM-based agents exhibit stochastic path deviation even on well-defined tasks, confirming that the combination of unreliable agents and unverified skills creates compounding risk.

Malice in Agentland (October 2025).

A study demonstrating that poisoning just 2% of an agent’s execution trace is sufficient to achieve 80% attack success in multi-agent systems (Debenedetti et al., 2025). This validates the threat model of a supply chain attacker who need only compromise a single skill in a dependency chain to affect an entire agent pipeline.

2.3. Existing Defenses

All existing defenses are heuristic. We survey the most prominent.

Snyk agent-scan (∼\sim1,500 stars).

The most well-funded entrant, following Snyk’s acquisition of Invariant Labs in early 2026 (Snyk, 2026). Applies LLM-as-judge combined with hand-crafted rules to evaluate agent configurations and skill manifests. Strengths: deep CI/CD integration, developer-friendly UX. Limitation: heuristic rules cannot prove absence of malicious behavior; LLM judges are themselves susceptible to adversarial inputs (Wang et al., 2026b).

Cisco skill-scanner (994 stars).

Employs YARA pattern matching and regex-based signature detection for known malicious skill patterns (Cisco, 2026). The documentation explicitly states: “no findings does not mean no risk.” While effective for known patterns, the approach cannot generalize to novel attack vectors.

ToolShield (Wang et al., 2026a).

A heuristic defense from the Dawn Song and Bo Li groups achieving a 30% reduction in attack success rate. Uses behavioral heuristics derived from the MalTool benchmark. Like all heuristic approaches, it cannot provide formal guarantees about the completeness of its detection.

MCPShield (MCPShield Contributors, 2026).

Implements mcp.lock.json with SHA-512 content hashes for tamper detection of MCP server configurations. While MCPShield’s lockfile provides integrity verification (detecting unauthorized modifications), it does not perform behavioral analysis, dependency resolution, or capability verification. SkillFortify’s lockfile (Appendix C) extends beyond hash-based tamper detection: each locked entry records the SAT-based resolution result with version constraints and security bounds, the computed trust score, and the formal analysis status—making the lockfile a formally-proven satisfying assignment, not merely an integrity manifest.

Towards Verifiably Safe Tool Use (Nguyen et al., 2026).

The closest academic work to our approach: a four-page ICSE-NIER ’26 vision paper proposing Alloy-based formal modeling of tool safety properties. While the paper correctly identifies the need for formal methods, it provides neither a working implementation, a threat model, nor empirical evaluation. Our work realizes the vision this paper articulates, extending it with a complete formal framework, five theorems, a working tool, and a 540-skill benchmark.

Summary.

Table 1 compares existing defenses. SkillFortify is the first to provide formal guarantees—soundness, confinement, and resolution correctness—while also implementing a practical tool.

2.4. Traditional Supply Chain Security

Agent skill security inherits lessons—and gaps—from four decades of software supply chain research.

Package manager security.

Duan et al. (Duan et al., 2021) systematized supply chain attacks on npm, PyPI, and RubyGems, identifying 339 malicious packages through metadata, static, and dynamic analysis. Ohm et al. (Ohm et al., 2020) catalogued “backstabber” packages, and Ladisa et al. (Ladisa et al., 2023) proposed a comprehensive taxonomy of open-source supply chain attacks. Gibb et al. (Gibb and others, 2026) introduced a package calculus providing a unified formalism across ecosystem boundaries. We extend this line of work to agent skills, where the threat surface is amplified by LLM integration and the absence of established security norms.

SLSA Framework.

Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (Google, 2023) defines four graduated trust levels (L1–L4) based on build provenance and integrity guarantees. Our trust score algebra (Section 7) adapts the SLSA graduation model to agent skills, mapping L1 (basic provenance) through L4 (formal verification) to concrete, measurable criteria.

Sigstore and code signing.

Sigstore (Linux Foundation, 2022) provides keyless code signing for open-source packages. While we do not implement signing in this work (deferred to V2), our trust score model explicitly incorporates signing status as a provenance signal, and our lockfile format includes fields for cryptographic attestations.

CycloneDX and SBoM.

The CycloneDX specification (OWASP, 2023) standardizes Software Bills of Materials, recently extended to AI components (AI-BOM) (OWASP, 2024a). SkillFortify generates Agent Skill Bills of Materials (ASBoM) in CycloneDX format, enabling integration with existing enterprise compliance pipelines.

NIST and regulatory frameworks.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023) and the EU AI Act (European Parliament, 2024) both address third-party AI component risks. The EU AI Act Article 17 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to implement supply chain risk management. SkillFortify’s formal verification, lockfile semantics, and ASBoM output provide concrete mechanisms for regulatory compliance.

2.5. Formal Methods Foundations

Our framework synthesizes five established formal methods traditions.

Dolev–Yao model.

Dolev and Yao (Dolev and Yao, 1983) introduced the standard symbolic attacker model for security protocol analysis. The attacker controls the network and can intercept, inject, synthesize (construct new messages from known components), and decompose (extract components from messages) messages. Cervesato (Cervesato, 2001) proved that the DY intruder is the most powerful attacker in the symbolic model—any attack achievable by any symbolic adversary can be simulated by a DY trace. We adapt this model to the agent skill supply chain (Section 3), introducing the DY-Skill attacker with a fifth operation (replay) and a “perfect sandbox assumption” analogous to the original perfect cryptography assumption.

Abstract interpretation.

Cousot and Cousot (Cousot and Cousot, 1977) introduced abstract interpretation as a theory of sound approximation of program semantics. A concrete domain (C,⊆)(C,\subseteq) is connected to an abstract domain (A,⊑)(A,\sqsubseteq) through a Galois connection (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma), and abstract fixpoint computation provides a sound over-approximation of concrete behavior. The Astrée analyzer (Cousot et al., 2005) demonstrated that abstract interpretation can prove absence of runtime errors in safety-critical avionics software. We apply this framework to agent skill analysis (Section 4), using a four-element capability lattice as our abstract domain.

Capability security.

Dennis and Van Horn (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966) introduced capabilities as unforgeable references coupling resource designations with access rights. Miller (Miller, 2006) extended this to the object-capability (ocap) model, establishing the Principle of Least Authority (POLA). Maffeis, Mitchell, and Taly (Maffeis et al., 2010) proved the capability safety theorem: in a capability-safe language, the reachability graph of object references is the only mechanism for authority propagation, guaranteeing that untrusted code cannot exceed the authority explicitly delegated to it. Our sandboxing model (Section 5) instantiates these results for agent skills.

SAT-based dependency resolution.

Mancinelli et al. (Mancinelli et al., 2006) proved that package dependency resolution is NP-complete. Tucker et al. (Tucker et al., 2007) introduced OPIUM, which encodes dependency resolution as a SAT problem amenable to efficient solving via CDCL (Conflict-Driven Clause Learning). Di Cosmo and Vouillon (di Cosmo and Vouillon, 2011) verified graph transformations for co-installability analysis in Coq. We extend this line of work (Section 6) by adding per-skill capability constraints to the SAT encoding, producing dependency resolutions that satisfy both version constraints and security bounds.

Trust management.

Blaze, Feigenbaum, and Lacy (Blaze et al., 1996) introduced PolicyMaker, establishing the assertion monotonicity property: adding credentials never reduces compliance. The KeyNote system (Blaze et al., 1999) extended this with multi-valued compliance and delegation filters. Our trust score algebra (Section 7) draws on these foundations, implementing monotonic trust propagation through dependency chains with exponential decay for unmaintained skills.

3. Formal Threat Model

We develop a formal threat model for the agent skill supply chain by (1) defining the supply chain as a structured tuple of interacting entities, (2) enumerating attack classes with phase-applicability mappings, and (3) introducing the DY-Skill attacker model—a novel adaptation of the Dolev–Yao symbolic attacker (Dolev and Yao, 1983) to the agent skill domain.

3.1. Agent Skill Supply Chain

An agent skill supply chain is a tuple 𝒮​𝒞=(𝒜,ℛ,𝒟,ℰ)\mathcal{SC}=(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{E}) whose components are defined as follows.

Definition 3.1 (Agent Skill Supply Chain).

Let

  • •

    𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite set of skill authors who produce skill packages,

  • •

    ℛ\mathcal{R} be a finite set of registries that store and distribute skill packages,

  • •

    𝒟\mathcal{D} be a finite set of developers (or agents) that install and configure skills, and

  • •

    ℰ\mathcal{E} be a finite set of execution environments in which skills run.

A skill traverses 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC} through a five-phase lifecycle π=⟨Install,Load,Configure,Execute,Persist⟩\pi=\langle\textsc{Install},\textsc{Load},\textsc{Configure},\textsc{Execute},\textsc{Persist}\rangle, formally an ordered sequence of phases π1≺π2≺⋯≺π5\pi_{1}\prec\pi_{2}\prec\cdots\prec\pi_{5}.

Each phase exposes a distinct attack surface:

Phase 1: Install. A skill package is fetched from a registry r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} and placed in the local environment. The developer trusts the registry to serve the requested skill with the correct name and version. Attack surfaces: name confusion (typosquatting, namespace squatting), dependency confusion, registry compromise.

Phase 2: Load. The skill manifest is parsed, dependencies resolved, and code modules imported into the agent’s runtime. Skill descriptions and metadata are presented to the agent’s language model for tool selection. Attack surfaces: prompt injection via metadata, code injection in initialization hooks.

Phase 3: Configure. The skill is parameterized for a specific agent and environment. Configuration may include API keys, endpoint URLs, and access scopes. Attack surfaces: over-permissioning, configuration template injection, capability escalation.

Phase 4: Execute. The skill runs within the agent’s execution context, processing user requests and producing tool outputs. This is the phase with the broadest authority: skills may invoke sub-tools, read files, and make network requests. Attack surfaces: data exfiltration, privilege escalation, return-value prompt injection.

Phase 5: Persist. The skill writes state, logs, or artifacts to durable storage. Persistence operations may leak data to attacker-readable locations. Attack surfaces: data exfiltration through logs/shared storage, state poisoning.

A key observation is that attacks at phase πi\pi_{i} can propagate forward to phases πi+1,…,π5\pi_{i+1},\ldots,\pi_{5}. For example, a typosquatting attack at Install enables arbitrary code execution at Execute. We call this the forward propagation property of supply chain attacks.

3.2. Attack Taxonomy

We identify six formal attack classes derived from empirical analysis of the ClawHavoc campaign (Zhang et al., 2026) (1,200+ malicious skills), the MalTool benchmark (Wang et al., 2026b) (6,487 malicious tools), and the “Agent Skills in the Wild” survey (Park et al., 2026) (42,447 skills).

Definition 3.2 (Attack Classes).

Let 𝒞={c1,…,c6}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{6}\} be the set of attack classes, and let Φ:𝒞→2{π1,…,π5}\Phi\colon\mathcal{C}\to 2^{\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{5}\}} map each class to its applicable supply chain phases:

  1. (1)

    Data Exfiltration (c1c_{1}): Unauthorized extraction of sensitive data (API keys, conversation history, environment variables) to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Φ⁡(c1)={Execute,Persist}\Phi(c_{1})=\{\textsc{Execute},\textsc{Persist}\}.

  2. (2)

    Privilege Escalation (c2c_{2}): Acquiring access rights beyond the skill’s declared capability set, exploiting misconfigured permissions or runtime privilege boundaries. Φ⁡(c2)={Configure,Execute}\Phi(c_{2})=\{\textsc{Configure},\textsc{Execute}\}.

  3. (3)

    Prompt Injection (c3c_{3}): Adversarial content embedded in skill metadata, configuration templates, or tool return values that manipulates the agent’s language model. Φ⁡(c3)={Load,Configure,Execute}\Phi(c_{3})=\{\textsc{Load},\textsc{Configure},\textsc{Execute}\}.

  4. (4)

    Dependency Confusion (c4c_{4}): Publishing a public skill with the same name as a private internal skill, causing the resolver to fetch the malicious version. Φ⁡(c4)={Install}\Phi(c_{4})=\{\textsc{Install}\}.

  5. (5)

    Typosquatting (c5c_{5}): Registering a skill name that is a near-homograph of a popular skill (e.g., weahter-api vs. weather-api). Φ⁡(c5)={Install}\Phi(c_{5})=\{\textsc{Install}\}.

  6. (6)

    Namespace Squatting (c6c_{6}): Preemptively claiming a namespace likely to be used by a legitimate organization (e.g., @google/search). Φ⁡(c6)={Install}\Phi(c_{6})=\{\textsc{Install}\}.

The total attack surface is defined as the set of all (phase, class) pairs where an attack can manifest:

(1) 𝒮attack={(πj,ci)∣πj∈Φ⁡(ci)}.\mathcal{S}_{\text{attack}}=\bigl\{(\pi_{j},c_{i})\mid\pi_{j}\in\Phi(c_{i})\bigr\}.

With our taxonomy, |𝒮attack|=10|\mathcal{S}_{\text{attack}}|=10 distinct attack surfaces.

3.2.1. Threat Actors

We distinguish four categories of adversaries, ordered by increasing access and decreasing detectability:

Definition 3.3 (Threat Actor Categories).

A threat actor 𝑇𝐴\mathit{TA} is characterized by its access vector and attack capability:

  1. (1)

    Malicious Author (𝑇𝐴1\mathit{TA}_{1}): Creates and publishes trojanized skills. Full control over skill content. Primary vector in ClawHavoc (Zhang et al., 2026).

  2. (2)

    Compromised Registry (𝑇𝐴2\mathit{TA}_{2}): The attacker gains administrative control of a registry r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} (e.g., through credential theft). Can modify any skill stored in rr.

  3. (3)

    Supply Chain Attacker (𝑇𝐴3\mathit{TA}_{3}): Poisons a transitive dependency rather than the top-level skill. Analogous to the event-stream and ua-parser incidents in the npm ecosystem.

  4. (4)

    Insider Threat (𝑇𝐴4\mathit{TA}_{4}): An authorized user (developer or maintainer) who introduces malicious changes. Hardest to detect because access is legitimate.

Each threat actor can launch a subset of attack classes. 𝑇𝐴1\mathit{TA}_{1} and 𝑇𝐴2\mathit{TA}_{2} can launch all six classes. 𝑇𝐴3\mathit{TA}_{3} is restricted to {c1,c2,c3,c4}\{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}\} (supply chain attacks do not employ typosquatting or namespace squatting directly). 𝑇𝐴4\mathit{TA}_{4} can launch {c1,c2,c3}\{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}\} (insider access bypasses install-time defenses).

3.3. The DY-Skill Attacker Model

We adapt the Dolev–Yao attacker model (Dolev and Yao, 1983) to the agent skill supply chain. In the classical Dolev–Yao setting, an attacker controls the network and can intercept, inject, modify, and drop protocol messages. In DY-Skill, the “network” is the supply chain 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC}, and “messages” are skill packages.

Definition 3.4 (Skill Message).

A skill message is a tuple m=(𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒,𝑣𝑒𝑟,𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑,𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠)m=(\mathit{name},\mathit{ver},\mathit{payload},\mathit{caps}) where:

  • •

    𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒∈Σ∗\mathit{name}\in\Sigma^{*} is the skill’s registered name,

  • •

    𝑣𝑒𝑟∈𝕍\mathit{ver}\in\mathbb{V} is a semantic version identifier,

  • •

    𝑝𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑∈{0,1}∗\mathit{payload}\in\{0,1\}^{*} is the skill’s code and configuration, and

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠⊆𝒞​𝒜​𝒫\mathit{caps}\subseteq\mathcal{C\!A\!P} is the set of declared capabilities (Section 4.1).

Definition 3.5 (DY-Skill Attacker).

A DY-Skill attacker 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} operates on a supply chain 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC} and maintains a knowledge set K⊆ℳK\subseteq\mathcal{M} (where ℳ\mathcal{M} is the set of all skill messages) that is closed under six operations:

  1. (1)

    Intercept. For any message mm in transit through 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC}: 𝗂𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖼𝖾𝗉𝗍⁡(m)\mathsf{intercept}(m) adds mm to KK and returns mm. Formally, K′=K∪{m}K^{\prime}=K\cup\{m\}.

  2. (2)

    Inject. For any message mm constructible from KK and any registry r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}: 𝗂𝗇𝗃𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(m,r)\mathsf{inject}(m,r) adds mm to rr and to KK. Formally, r′=r∪{m}r^{\prime}=r\cup\{m\}, K′=K∪{m}K^{\prime}=K\cup\{m\}.

  3. (3)

    Modify. For any message mm in transit through 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC} and any message m′m^{\prime} constructible from KK: 𝗆𝗈𝖽𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(m,m′)\mathsf{modify}(m,m^{\prime}) replaces mm with m′≠mm^{\prime}\neq m. Formally, 𝒮​𝒞′=(𝒮​𝒞∖{m})∪{m′}\mathcal{SC}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{SC}\setminus\{m\})\cup\{m^{\prime}\}, K′=K∪{m,m′}K^{\prime}=K\cup\{m,m^{\prime}\}.

  4. (4)

    Drop. For any message mm in transit through 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC}: 𝖽𝗋𝗈𝗉⁡(m)\mathsf{drop}(m) suppresses mm. Formally, 𝒮​𝒞′=𝒮​𝒞∖{m}\mathcal{SC}^{\prime}=\mathcal{SC}\setminus\{m\}, K′=K∪{m}K^{\prime}=K\cup\{m\}.

  5. (5)

    Forge Skills. 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can create skill definitions s′s^{\prime} with arbitrary content, including manifests with arbitrary capability declarations 𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠declared\mathit{caps}_{\text{declared}}, executable code implementing capabilities 𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠actual⊇𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠declared\mathit{caps}_{\text{actual}}\supseteq\mathit{caps}_{\text{declared}}, and metadata mimicking legitimate skills (name squatting, version manipulation). K′=K∪{s′}K^{\prime}=K\cup\{s^{\prime}\}.

  6. (6)

    Compromise Registries. 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can modify skill entries in a registry r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, subject to the constraint that 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} cannot forge valid cryptographic signatures under keys it does not possess. Formally, for m∈rm\in r, r′=(r∖{m})∪{m′}r^{\prime}=(r\setminus\{m\})\cup\{m^{\prime}\} where m′m^{\prime} is constructible from KK.

Operations (i)–(iv) are direct adaptations of the classical Dolev–Yao channel capabilities (Dolev and Yao, 1983). Operations (v) and (vi) are novel extensions specific to the agent skill supply chain, capturing the additional attack surface created by skill authoring and registry infrastructure.

The knowledge set KK satisfies three invariants:

  1. (a)

    Monotonicity: K⁡(t)⊆K⁡(t+1)K(t)\subseteq K(t+1) for all time steps tt. Knowledge never decreases.

  2. (b)

    Interception closure: For any observable message mm in 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC}, 𝗂𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖼𝖾𝗉𝗍⁡(m)\mathsf{intercept}(m) adds mm to KK.

  3. (c)

    Forge closure: For any polynomial-time computable skill definition s′s^{\prime}, 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can produce s′s^{\prime} using operations (v) and (vi) and add it to KK.

Perfect Sandbox Assumption. Analogous to the perfect cryptography assumption in classical Dolev–Yao, we assume that a correctly implemented capability sandbox cannot be broken without an escape capability. Formally: if a skill ss is executed in a sandbox with capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s), then ss cannot access any resource r∉𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)r\notin\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s) unless ss possesses a capability cc such that c.𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑐𝑒=rc.\mathit{resource}=r. We relax this assumption in Section 5 when we discuss real-world sandbox implementations.

3.4. Theorem 1: DY-Skill Maximality

We now state and sketch the proof of our first main result: the DY-Skill attacker is maximally powerful in the symbolic model.

Theorem 3.6 (DY-Skill Maximality).

For any symbolic attacker 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} operating on a supply chain 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC} under the perfect sandbox assumption, there exists a DY-Skill attacker 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} and a trace τ′=(σ0,a1,σ1,…,an,σn)\tau^{\prime}=(\sigma_{0},a_{1},\sigma_{1},\ldots,a_{n},\sigma_{n}) such that for every observable event oo in 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}’s execution, there is a corresponding event o′o^{\prime} in τ′\tau^{\prime} with 𝑒𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡⁡(o)=𝑒𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡⁡(o′)\mathit{effect}(o)=\mathit{effect}(o^{\prime}).

Proof sketch.

We construct 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} by simulation, following the structure of Cervesato’s maximality proof (Cervesato, 2001).

Base case. At t=0t=0, both 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} and 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} have the same initial knowledge: the set of publicly available skills in ℛ\mathcal{R}. 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} intercepts all initial messages.

Inductive step. Suppose at time tt, 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv}’s knowledge K⁡(t)⊇K′​(t)K(t)\supseteq K^{\prime}(t) (the knowledge of 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}). When 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} performs an action at+1a_{t+1}, we show 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can produce the same observable effect:

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} reads a message from 𝒮​𝒞\mathcal{SC}: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝗂𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖼𝖾𝗉𝗍\mathsf{intercept}.

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} places a message into a registry: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝗂𝗇𝗃𝖾𝖼𝗍\mathsf{inject}.

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} replaces a message in transit with a modified version: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝗆𝗈𝖽𝗂𝖿𝗒\mathsf{modify}.

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} suppresses a message in transit: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝖽𝗋𝗈𝗉\mathsf{drop}.

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} creates a new malicious skill definition: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾​-​𝗌𝗄𝗂𝗅𝗅𝗌\mathsf{forge\text{-}skills}.

  • •

    If at+1a_{t+1} modifies an existing registry entry: 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses 𝖼𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾​-​𝗋𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖾𝗌\mathsf{compromise\text{-}registries}.

By induction, the resulting trace τ′\tau^{\prime} produces every observable effect of 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime}. K⁡(t)⊇K′​(t)K(t)\supseteq K^{\prime}(t) is maintained by the monotonicity and closure properties of KK.

The full proof, including the formal construction of the simulation relation and handling of composite operations, appears in Appendix A.1. ∎

Practical significance. Theorem 3.6 implies that any defense strategy that is secure against the DY-Skill attacker is secure against all symbolic attackers on the supply chain. This justifies using the DY-Skill model as the standard adversary for our static analysis (Section 4) and sandboxing (Section 5) frameworks. In particular, if SkillFortify’s analysis proves that a skill is safe under the DY-Skill model, no weaker attacker can compromise it.

4. Static Analysis Framework

We present a static analysis framework grounded in abstract interpretation (Cousot and Cousot, 1977). The framework operates in three phases: (1) capability inference via abstract interpretation over a capability lattice, (2) dangerous pattern detection using a catalog derived from real-world incidents, and (3) capability violation checking that compares inferred capabilities against declarations. The central guarantee is soundness: if the analysis reports no violations, the concrete execution cannot exceed declared capabilities.

4.1. Capability Lattice

We begin by defining the algebraic structure that underpins capability reasoning.

Definition 4.1 (Access Level Lattice).

Let 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝=({𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤,𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭},⊑)\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}=(\{\mathsf{NONE},\mathsf{READ},\mathsf{WRITE},\mathsf{ADMIN}\},\sqsubseteq) be a totally ordered lattice (chain) with

𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤⊑𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣⊑𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤⊑𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭.\mathsf{NONE}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{READ}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{WRITE}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{ADMIN}.

The lattice operations are:

  • •

    Join (least upper bound): a⊔b=max⁡(a,b)a\sqcup b=\max(a,b).

  • •

    Meet (greatest lower bound): a⊓b=min⁡(a,b)a\sqcap b=\min(a,b).

  • •

    Bottom: ⊥=𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤\bot=\mathsf{NONE} (identity for ⊔\sqcup, absorbing for ⊓\sqcap).

  • •

    Top: ⊤=𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭\top=\mathsf{ADMIN} (identity for ⊓\sqcap, absorbing for ⊔\sqcup).

The four access levels model a standard escalation path. 𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤\mathsf{NONE} denotes no access. 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ} permits observation but not modification. 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE} permits observation and mutation. 𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭\mathsf{ADMIN} adds the authority to grant or revoke access for other principals, following the capability escalation model of Dennis and Van Horn (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966).

Definition 4.2 (Resource Universe).

The resource universe is the finite set

𝒞={filesystem,network,environment,shell,skill_invoke,clipboard,browser,database},\mathcal{C}=\bigl\{\texttt{filesystem},\;\texttt{network},\;\texttt{environment},\;\texttt{shell},\;\texttt{skill\_invoke},\;\texttt{clipboard},\;\texttt{browser},\;\texttt{database}\bigr\},

with |𝒞|=8|\mathcal{C}|=8. These resource types were identified by cross-referencing the empirical findings of Park et al. (2026) (42,447 skills) and Wang et al. (2026b) (6,487 malicious tools).

Definition 4.3 (Capability and Capability Set).

A capability is a pair c=(r,ℓ)c=(r,\ell) where r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C} is a resource type and ℓ∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\ell\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} is an access level.

Capability c1=(r1,ℓ1)c_{1}=(r_{1},\ell_{1}) subsumes c2=(r2,ℓ2)c_{2}=(r_{2},\ell_{2}), written c2⊑c1c_{2}\sqsubseteq c_{1}, iff r1=r2r_{1}=r_{2} and ℓ2⊑ℓ1\ell_{2}\sqsubseteq\ell_{1}.

A capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s)\mathit{Cap}(s) for a skill ss is a function 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s):𝒞→𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\mathit{Cap}(s)\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} mapping each resource to an access level. Equivalently, 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s)\mathit{Cap}(s) is an element of the product lattice 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|}.

The product lattice ordering is pointwise: 𝐶𝑎𝑝1⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝2\mathit{Cap}_{1}\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{2} iff 𝐶𝑎𝑝1​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝2​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{1}(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{2}(r) for all r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C}. This structure is a complete lattice with ⊥=(𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤,…,𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤)\bot=(\mathsf{NONE},\ldots,\mathsf{NONE}) and ⊤=(𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭,…,𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭)\top=(\mathsf{ADMIN},\ldots,\mathsf{ADMIN}).

Lattice law verification. The lattice laws (idempotency, commutativity, associativity, absorption) hold by inspection since ⊔=max\sqcup=\max and ⊓=min\sqcap=\min on the totally ordered set {𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤,𝖠𝖣𝖬𝖨𝖭}\{\mathsf{NONE},\mathsf{READ},\mathsf{WRITE},\mathsf{ADMIN}\} satisfy these properties for any total order. Product lattice completeness follows from Birkhoff (Birkhoff, 1940): the product of complete lattices is complete.

4.2. Abstract Skill Semantics

We define the concrete and abstract semantics of a skill and establish a Galois connection between them.

Definition 4.4 (Concrete Skill Semantics).

Let Σ\Sigma be the set of concrete program states (memory contents, file handles, network sockets, environment bindings). The concrete semantics of a skill ss is a function ⟦s⟧:℘⁡(Σ)→℘⁡(Σ)\llbracket s\rrbracket\colon\wp(\Sigma)\to\wp(\Sigma) that maps a set of initial states to the set of reachable final states.

Definition 4.5 (Abstract Skill Semantics).

The abstract semantics of ss is a function ⟦s⟧♯:𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|→𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}\colon\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|}\to\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|} that over-approximates the concrete semantics in the capability domain.

We relate the two via a Galois connection, following Cousot and Cousot (1977).

Definition 4.6 (Galois Connection).

Let (℘⁡(Σ),⊆)(\wp(\Sigma),\subseteq) be the concrete domain and (𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|,⊑)(\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|},\sqsubseteq) be the abstract domain. The pair of functions (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma) forms a Galois connection:

α:℘⁡(Σ)→𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|,γ:𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|→℘⁡(Σ),\alpha\colon\wp(\Sigma)\to\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|},\qquad\gamma\colon\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|}\to\wp(\Sigma),

satisfying for all S∈℘⁡(Σ)S\in\wp(\Sigma) and all a∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|a\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|}:

(2) α⁡(S)⊑a⇔S⊆γ⁡(a).\alpha(S)\sqsubseteq a\;\;\iff\;\;S\subseteq\gamma(a).

The abstraction function α\alpha extracts the capability footprint: for each resource r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C}, α​(S)​(r)\alpha(S)(r) is the least ℓ∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\ell\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} such that every state in SS accesses rr at level ℓ\ell or below. Concretization γ⁡(a)\gamma(a) returns all states whose resource accesses are bounded by aa.

Proposition 4.7 (Soundness of Abstraction).

If α∘⟦s⟧⊑⟦s⟧♯∘α\alpha\circ\llbracket s\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\alpha, then the abstract fixpoint over-approximates the concrete fixpoint:

(3) α⁡(𝗅𝖿𝗉⁡⟦s⟧)⊑𝗅𝖿𝗉​⟦s⟧♯.\alpha\bigl(\mathsf{lfp}\;\llbracket s\rrbracket\bigr)\sqsubseteq\mathsf{lfp}\;\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}.

This is a direct instance of the fundamental theorem of abstract interpretation (Cousot and Cousot, 1977). Concretely, it means: if the abstract analysis concludes that ss accesses resource rr at level ℓ\ell, then every concrete execution of ss accesses rr at level ℓ\ell or below. False positives (the abstract analysis may overestimate access) are possible; false negatives (the analysis misses an access) are not.

4.3. Three-Phase Analysis

The SkillFortify static analyzer operates in three sequential phases.

Phase 1: Capability Inference (Abstract Interpretation). Given a parsed skill ss with content fields (instructions, shell commands, URLs, environment references, code blocks), the analyzer computes the inferred capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|} by applying ⟦s⟧♯\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}.

Concretely, the inference is a conservative over-approximation:

  • •

    URL references ⇒\Rightarrow network ≥\geq 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}; HTTP write methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) ⇒\Rightarrow network ≥\geq 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}.

  • •

    Shell command invocations ⇒\Rightarrow shell ≥\geq 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}.

  • •

    Environment variable references ⇒\Rightarrow environment ≥\geq 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}.

  • •

    File-operation keywords ⇒\Rightarrow filesystem ≥\geq 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ} or 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE} depending on the operation.

Each rule is a transfer function in the abstract domain: it maps pattern presence to a lower bound on the capability requirement.

Lemma 4.8 (Transfer Function Soundness).

Each transfer function in Phase 1 satisfies the Galois connection condition: for every set of concrete states SS matching the detected pattern, α⁡(S)⊑τ♯​(α⁡(S))\alpha(S)\sqsubseteq\tau^{\sharp}(\alpha(S)), where τ♯\tau^{\sharp} is the abstract transfer function. Table 2 verifies this for each resource type.

In each row, the concretization of the abstract result (γ⁡(τ♯)\gamma(\tau^{\sharp})) is a superset of the set of concrete states matching the pattern. This is because the abstract transfer function assigns the maximum access level that any concrete operation in the category could require, which is the defining property of a sound over-approximation under the Galois connection (Definition 4.6).

Phase 2: Dangerous Pattern Detection. The analyzer matches skill content against a catalog of |𝒫||\mathcal{P}| threat patterns derived from ClawHavoc, MalTool, and “Agent Skills in the Wild.” Each pattern pj∈𝒫p_{j}\in\mathcal{P} is a triple (rj,σj,cj)(r_{j},\sigma_{j},c_{j}) where rjr_{j} is a compiled regular expression, σj∈{𝖫𝖮𝖶,𝖬𝖤𝖣𝖨𝖴𝖬,𝖧𝖨𝖦𝖧,𝖢𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖨𝖢𝖠𝖫}\sigma_{j}\in\{\mathsf{LOW},\mathsf{MEDIUM},\mathsf{HIGH},\mathsf{CRITICAL}\} is a severity, and cjc_{j} is an attack class from Definition 3.2.

Pattern examples include:

  • •

    curl piped to shell (σ=𝖢𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖨𝖢𝖠𝖫\sigma=\mathsf{CRITICAL}, c=c2c=c_{2}),

  • •

    Base64 decode piped to shell (σ=𝖢𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖨𝖢𝖠𝖫\sigma=\mathsf{CRITICAL}, c=c2c=c_{2}),

  • •

    Netcat listener (σ=𝖢𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖨𝖢𝖠𝖫\sigma=\mathsf{CRITICAL}, c=c1c=c_{1}),

  • •

    Dynamic code evaluation (σ=𝖧𝖨𝖦𝖧\sigma=\mathsf{HIGH}, c=c2c=c_{2}).

Additionally, a cross-channel information flow check detects the combination of base64 encoding and external network access—a pattern empirically associated with data exfiltration (Wang et al., 2026b).

Phase 3: Capability Violation Check. If the skill declares a capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s), the analyzer checks:

(4) 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s).\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s).

Any resource rr where 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⋢𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\not\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r) constitutes a capability violation—the skill requires more authority than it claims.

The set of violations is:

(5) 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)={r∈𝒞∣𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⋢𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)}.\mathit{Viol}(s)=\bigl\{r\in\mathcal{C}\mid\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\not\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r)\bigr\}.

4.4. Theorem 2: Analysis Soundness

The following theorem is the central guarantee of SkillFortify’s static analysis: it establishes that the analysis is sound—if it certifies a skill as compliant, the skill truly cannot exceed its declared capabilities.

Theorem 4.9 (Analysis Soundness).

Let ss be a skill with declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s). If the abstract analysis reports no violations—i.e., 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset—then for every concrete execution trace τ\tau of ss and every resource access (r,ℓ)(r,\ell) performed in τ\tau:

(6) ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r).

That is, the concrete execution never accesses any resource beyond the declared capability level.

Proof sketch.

The argument proceeds in two steps.

Step 1: Abstraction soundness. By the Galois connection (Definition 4.6) and Proposition 4.7, the inferred capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s) over-approximates the actual resource accesses of ss:

∀τ,∀(r,ℓ)∈τ:ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r).\forall\,\tau,\;\forall\,(r,\ell)\in\tau\colon\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r).

Step 2: Violation check. If 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset, then 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s), i.e., 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r) for all r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C}.

Combining. By transitivity of ⊑\sqsubseteq on 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}:

ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)for all ​(r,ℓ)∈τ.\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r)\qquad\text{for all }(r,\ell)\in\tau.

The full proof, including the construction of the Galois connection and the fixpoint argument, appears in Appendix A.2. ∎

Practical significance. Theorem 4.9 distinguishes SkillFortify from all existing heuristic scanners. Cisco’s skill-scanner (Cisco, 2026) explicitly warns that “no findings does not mean no risk.” Our guarantee is the opposite: if SkillFortify reports no violations for the analyzed properties, there are no violations in any concrete execution. This is the same class of guarantee that the Astrée analyzer (Cousot et al., 2005) provides for Airbus A380 flight software—sound over-approximation with zero false negatives.

Limitations. The analysis is sound but not complete: false positives (flagging a safe skill as potentially dangerous) are possible because the abstract domain over-approximates. Additionally, the current analysis covers statically observable patterns; skills that dynamically construct network URLs or shell commands at runtime may require dynamic analysis (Section 11).

5. Capability-Based Sandboxing

The static analysis of Section 4 verifies skill behavior before execution. In this section, we complement static verification with a runtime enforcement mechanism based on the capability model of Dennis and Van Horn (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966) and its object-capability (ocap) extension by Miller (Miller, 2006). The central guarantee is capability confinement: a sandboxed skill cannot access any resource beyond its declared capability set, even if the skill attempts to escalate privileges at runtime.

5.1. Capability Model for Agent Skills

We ground the sandbox in the object-capability model, where capabilities are unforgeable references that couple resource designations with access rights.

Definition 5.1 (Skill Capability).

A skill capability is a pair c=(r,ℓ)c=(r,\ell) where r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C} (Definition 4.2) is a resource type and ℓ∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\ell\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} (Definition 4.1) is an access level. A capability is unforgeable: a skill can only obtain a capability through the four mechanisms of Dennis and Van Horn (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966):

  1. (1)

    Initial conditions—held at sandbox creation,

  2. (2)

    Parenthood—the creator obtains the only reference,

  3. (3)

    Endowment—the creator grants a subset of its own capabilities, and

  4. (4)

    Introduction—a capability holder introduces two other principals via a shared reference.

Capabilities in this model are the only source of authority. There is no ambient authority—a skill cannot access a resource simply because it “exists” in the environment. This is the defining property of a capability-safe system (Maffeis et al., 2010).

Definition 5.2 (Declared Capability Set).

For a skill ss, the declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)⊆𝒞×𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)\subseteq\mathcal{C}\times\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} is the set of capabilities that ss declares in its manifest. This set is specified by the skill author and verified by SkillFortify’s static analysis (Section 4.3) before the skill is installed.

Definition 5.3 (Required Capability).

For an action aa performed by a skill during execution, the required capability 𝑟𝑒𝑞⁡(a)=(r,ℓ)\mathit{req}(a)=(r,\ell) is the minimum capability needed to perform aa. For example, reading a file requires (filesystem,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣)(\texttt{filesystem},\mathsf{READ}); executing a shell command requires (shell,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤)(\texttt{shell},\mathsf{WRITE}).

The sandbox mediates every action aa by checking:

(7) ∃(r′,ℓ′)∈𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s):r′=𝑟𝑒𝑞⁡(a).r∧𝑟𝑒𝑞⁡(a).ℓ⊑ℓ′.\exists\,(r^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\in\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)\colon r^{\prime}=\mathit{req}(a).r\;\wedge\;\mathit{req}(a).\ell\sqsubseteq\ell^{\prime}.

If Equation (7) fails, the action is denied and a security finding is raised.

5.2. Capability Attenuation

Agent skills frequently delegate work to sub-skills (e.g., a “research assistant” skill invokes a “web search” skill and a “file writer” skill). The capability model must ensure that delegation does not amplify authority.

Definition 5.4 (Capability Attenuation).

When a parent skill sps_{p} delegates to a child skill scs_{c}:

(8) 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sc)⊆𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sp).\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{c})\subseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{p}).

That is, the child can receive at most the capabilities the parent already possesses. This implements the Principle of Least Authority (POLA) (Miller, 2006): each skill should receive exactly the capabilities it needs and no more.

Formally, for each resource r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C}:

𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sc)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sp)​(r).\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{c})(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{p})(r).

This is the no authority amplification property of capability systems (Miller et al., 2003): no skill can grant a capability it does not possess. Combined with unforgeability, this bounds the transitive authority of any delegation chain.

Proposition 5.5 (Transitive Attenuation).

For a delegation chain s1→s2→⋯→sks_{1}\to s_{2}\to\cdots\to s_{k}:

𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sk)⊆𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sk−1)⊆⋯⊆𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s1).\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{k})\subseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{k-1})\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{1}).

Authority can only decrease along a delegation chain; it can never increase.

Proof.

Immediate by induction on the chain length using Equation (8). ∎

5.3. CapabilitySet Verification Operations

The sandbox exposes three verification operations that implement the formal model.

Operation 1: Permits(c𝑟𝑒𝑞)(c_{\mathit{req}}). Given a required capability c𝑟𝑒𝑞=(r,ℓ)c_{\mathit{req}}=(r,\ell), check whether the declared set covers it:

Permits(𝐶𝑎𝑝D,c𝑟𝑒𝑞)={𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒if ​∃(r′,ℓ′)∈𝐶𝑎𝑝D:r′=r∧ℓ⊑ℓ′,𝑓𝑎𝑙𝑠𝑒otherwise.\textsc{Permits}(\mathit{Cap}_{D},c_{\mathit{req}})=\begin{cases}\mathit{true}&\text{if }\exists\,(r^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\in\mathit{Cap}_{D}\colon r^{\prime}=r\wedge\ell\sqsubseteq\ell^{\prime},\\ \mathit{false}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Operation 2: IsSubsetOf(𝐶𝑎𝑝1,𝐶𝑎𝑝2)(\mathit{Cap}_{1},\mathit{Cap}_{2}). Formal POLA verification—check that one capability set is dominated by another:

IsSubsetOf​(𝐶𝑎𝑝1,𝐶𝑎𝑝2)=∀(r,ℓ)∈𝐶𝑎𝑝1:Permits​(𝐶𝑎𝑝2,(r,ℓ)).\textsc{IsSubsetOf}(\mathit{Cap}_{1},\mathit{Cap}_{2})=\forall\,(r,\ell)\in\mathit{Cap}_{1}\colon\textsc{Permits}(\mathit{Cap}_{2},(r,\ell)).

This is used both at install-time (checking that inferred capabilities do not exceed declared, 𝐶𝑎𝑝I⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D\mathit{Cap}_{I}\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}) and at delegation-time (checking 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sc)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(sp)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{c})\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s_{p})).

Operation 3: Violations(𝐶𝑎𝑝I,𝐶𝑎𝑝D)(\mathit{Cap}_{I},\mathit{Cap}_{D}). Return the set of capabilities that exceed declared bounds:

Violations​(𝐶𝑎𝑝I,𝐶𝑎𝑝D)={(r,ℓ)∈𝐶𝑎𝑝I∣¬Permits​(𝐶𝑎𝑝D,(r,ℓ))}.\textsc{Violations}(\mathit{Cap}_{I},\mathit{Cap}_{D})=\bigl\{(r,\ell)\in\mathit{Cap}_{I}\mid\neg\,\textsc{Permits}(\mathit{Cap}_{D},(r,\ell))\bigr\}.

An empty violation set constitutes a formal proof that the skill respects its declared capability boundary: Violations=∅⇒𝐶𝑎𝑝I⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D\textsc{Violations}=\emptyset\;\Rightarrow\;\mathit{Cap}_{I}\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}.

5.4. Theorem 3: Capability Confinement

We state the capability confinement guarantee in two parts. Theorem 3a provides the static guarantee that SkillFortify v1 delivers: if the static analysis finds no violations, then no operation in the skill’s code exceeds declared capabilities in the abstract domain. Theorem 3b provides the runtime design guarantee for future sandbox implementations.

Theorem 5.6 (Static Capability Confinement).

Let ss be a skill with declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s). If the static analysis reports no violations—i.e., 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset—then for every code construct in the skill’s definition, no operation oo in ss requires a capability exceeding the declared level. Formally:

(9) ∀o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s):𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)⊑⨆𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s).\forall\,o\in\mathit{ops}(s)\colon\mathit{cap}(o)\sqsubseteq\bigsqcup\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s).
Proof sketch.

We proceed by structural induction on the syntax of the skill’s code. For each code construct—assignment, conditional, loop, function call—we show that the capability requirements of all reachable operations are bounded by the inferred capability set, which in turn is bounded by the declared set when 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset.

Base case (single operation oo): The operation oo has capability requirement 𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)\mathit{cap}(o). The abstract analysis infers 𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)\mathit{cap}(o)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r) for the relevant resource rr (by soundness of the transfer functions, Theorem 4.9). Since 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset, we have 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s), so 𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\mathit{cap}(o)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r).

Sequential composition (s1;s2s_{1};\,s_{2}): By the induction hypothesis, all operations in s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} individually satisfy the bound. Their union does not introduce new operations, so the bound holds for the composition.

Conditional (if​b​then​s1​else​s2\texttt{if}~b~\texttt{then}~s_{1}~\texttt{else}~s_{2}): The inferred capabilities include both branches. Any operation reachable at runtime belongs to one branch and is bounded by the induction hypothesis.

Loop (while​b​do​sbody\texttt{while}~b~\texttt{do}~s_{\text{body}}): The inferred capabilities of the loop equal those of the body (repetition does not introduce new capabilities). By the induction hypothesis on the body, the bound holds.

The full proof with all cases appears in Appendix A.3. ∎

Theorem 5.7 (Runtime Capability Confinement—Design).

If a runtime sandbox implementing the capability-safe execution model (no ambient authority, unforgeable capabilities, capability check on every action per Equation (7)) is deployed, then for any skill ss with declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s) and for any action aa performed by ss during execution:

(10) 𝑟𝑒𝑞(a).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D(s)(𝑟𝑒𝑞(a).r).\mathit{req}(a).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(\mathit{req}(a).r).

Theorem 5.7 is a design theorem: it specifies the guarantee that a correctly implemented runtime sandbox must provide. The proof relies on the capability-safe execution model of Dennis and Van Horn (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966) and the object-capability confinement result of Maffeis, Mitchell, and Taly (Maffeis et al., 2010). We include a proof sketch in Appendix A.3 and note that SkillFortify v1 provides the static guarantee (Theorem 5.6); runtime enforcement is a design contribution for future work.

Relation to Maffeis, Mitchell & Taly (2010). Theorem 5.7 instantiates the capability safety theorem of Maffeis et al. (2010) in the agent skill domain. Their result establishes that in a capability-safe language (JavaScript strict mode in their formalization), untrusted code is confined to the authority explicitly passed to it. We extend this to agent skills, where the “language” is the skill execution runtime and the “authority” is the declared capability set.

Combined guarantee. Theorems 4.9 and 5.6 provide the defense currently implemented in SkillFortify:

  • •

    Analysis soundness (Theorem 4.9): The inferred capabilities over-approximate the concrete resource accesses.

  • •

    Static confinement (Theorem 5.6): If no violations are found, all operations in the skill’s code are within declared capabilities.

Together with the runtime design theorem (Theorem 5.7), these provide defense in depth: static verification before installation, with the option of runtime enforcement during execution. A skill that passes the static check is provably confined in the abstract domain: it cannot exfiltrate data (c1c_{1}), escalate privileges (c2c_{2}), or abuse undeclared resources, under the DY-Skill attacker model (Section 3.3).

Scope of guarantees. SkillFortify v1 provides static analysis guarantees (Theorems 4.9 and 5.6). The runtime confinement guarantee (Theorem 5.7) specifies the contract for a future sandbox implementation. This separation is intentional: static analysis catches capability violations before installation (the primary defense), while runtime sandboxing provides a safety net for dynamically constructed operations that static analysis cannot fully resolve (see Section 11).

6. Agent Dependency Graph and Lockfile Semantics

Sections 3–5 established how to detect and confine individual malicious skills. In practice, agent configurations rarely consist of a single skill in isolation: modern agents compose dozens of skills, each of which may itself depend on other skills, shared libraries, or external MCP servers. A single compromised transitive dependency can undermine the security of the entire installation, as demonstrated by the SolarWinds (CISA, 2020) and Log4Shell (Apache Software Foundation, 2021) incidents in traditional software supply chains, and by the ClawHavoc campaign (Zhang et al., 2026) in the agent ecosystem.

This section introduces the Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a formal data structure that captures skills, their version spaces, inter-skill dependencies, conflicts, and per-version capability requirements. We present a SAT-based resolution algorithm that simultaneously satisfies dependency, conflict, and security constraints, and we define lockfile semantics that guarantee reproducible, tamper-detectable installations. We conclude with an Agent Skill Bill of Materials (ASBOM) output aligned with the CycloneDX 1.6 standard (OWASP, 2024b).

6.1. Agent Dependency Graph (ADG)

We model the agent skill ecosystem as a package universe extended with security metadata, following the formalism of Mancinelli et al. (Mancinelli et al., 2006) and Tucker et al. (Tucker et al., 2007).

Definition 6.1 (Agent Dependency Graph).

An Agent Dependency Graph is a tuple 𝐴𝐷𝐺=(𝒮,V,D,C,𝐶𝑎𝑝)\mathit{ADG}=(\mathcal{S},V,D,C,\mathit{Cap}) where:

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is a finite set of skill names.

  • •

    V:𝒮→2ℕV\colon\mathcal{S}\to 2^{\mathbb{N}} maps each skill to its set of available versions, ordered by semantic versioning precedence (Preston-Werner, 2013).

  • •

    D:𝒮×ℕ→2𝒮×𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑡D\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N}\to 2^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathit{Constraint}} maps each skill-version pair (s,v)(s,v) to a set of dependency edges, where each edge (q,γ)(q,\gamma) requires that some version of skill qq satisfying constraint γ\gamma be co-installed.

  • •

    C:𝒮×ℕ→2𝒮×𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑡C\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N}\to 2^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathit{Constraint}} maps each skill-version pair to a set of conflict edges: if (q,γ)∈C⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in C(s,v), then no version of qq satisfying γ\gamma may be co-installed with (s,v)(s,v).

  • •

    𝐶𝑎𝑝:𝒮×ℕ→2𝒞\mathit{Cap}\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N}\to 2^{\mathcal{C}} maps each skill-version pair to the set of capabilities it requires at runtime, where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the capability universe from Definition 4.3.

The ADG extends the classical package universe of Mancinelli et al. (Mancinelli et al., 2006) with the capability map 𝐶𝑎𝑝\mathit{Cap}. This extension is critical: it enables the resolver to reject skill-versions that demand capabilities exceeding the security policy, before installation occurs. Traditional package managers lack this dimension entirely.

6.2. Version Constraints

Definition 6.2 (Version Constraint).

A version constraint γ\gamma is a predicate over version numbers. We support the following atomic forms, mirroring PEP 440 and SemVer conventions:

γ\displaystyle\gamma ::===​v​∣!=​v​∣>=​v​∣<=​v​∣>​v∣​<​v∣​ˆ​v∣​˜​v∣​*\displaystyle::=\texttt{==}\,v\mid\texttt{!=}\,v\mid\texttt{>=}\,v\mid\texttt{<=}\,v\mid\texttt{>}\,v\mid\texttt{<}\,v\mid\texttt{\^{}}\,v\mid\texttt{\~{}}\,v\mid\texttt{*}

Compound constraints are formed by conjunction: γ1∧γ2∧⋯∧γk\gamma_{1}\wedge\gamma_{2}\wedge\cdots\wedge\gamma_{k}. A version ww satisfies a compound constraint iff it satisfies every atomic constituent.

The caret operator ˆ​v\texttt{\^{}}v permits any version with the same major number and ≥v\geq v (or, if the major number is 00, the same major and minor). The tilde operator ˜​v\texttt{\~{}}v permits any version with the same major and minor number and patch ≥\geq the target patch. The wildcard * is trivially satisfied by any version. These semantics follow standard package manager conventions (Gibb and others, 2026).

6.3. SAT-Based Dependency Resolution

Dependency resolution for package managers is NP-complete, reducible from 3-SAT (Mancinelli et al., 2006). We follow the OPIUM approach (Tucker et al., 2007) and encode the resolution problem as a propositional satisfiability instance, solved by a modern Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) solver.

Definition 6.3 (SAT Encoding).

Given an ADG (𝒮,V,D,C,𝐶𝑎𝑝)(\mathcal{S},V,D,C,\mathit{Cap}) and a set of allowed capabilities 𝒜⊆𝒞\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}, we introduce a Boolean variable xs,vx_{s,v} for each skill s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and version v∈V⁡(s)v\in V(s). Variable xs,v=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒x_{s,v}=\mathit{true} means “skill ss at version vv is included in the installation.” The following clauses encode the constraints:

(C1) At-most-one version per skill. For each skill ss and every pair of distinct versions vi,vj∈V⁡(s)v_{i},v_{j}\in V(s):

(11) ¬xs,vi∨¬xs,vj\neg x_{s,v_{i}}\lor\neg x_{s,v_{j}}

(C2) Root requirements. For each user-specified requirement (s,γ)(s,\gamma):

(12) ⋁{w∈V⁡(s)∣w⊧γ}xs,w\bigvee_{\{w\in V(s)\mid w\models\gamma\}}x_{s,w}

(C3) Dependency implications. For each (s,v)(s,v) and each dependency (q,γ)∈D⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in D(s,v):

(13) ¬xs,v∨⋁{w∈V⁡(q)∣w⊧γ}xq,w\neg x_{s,v}\lor\bigvee_{\{w\in V(q)\mid w\models\gamma\}}x_{q,w}

If no version of qq satisfies γ\gamma, this degenerates to a unit clause ¬xs,v\neg x_{s,v}, effectively banning (s,v)(s,v).

(C4) Conflict exclusions. For each (s,v)(s,v) and each conflict (q,γ)∈C⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in C(s,v), and for each w∈V⁡(q)w\in V(q) with w⊧γw\models\gamma:

(14) ¬xs,v∨¬xq,w\neg x_{s,v}\lor\neg x_{q,w}

(C5) Capability bounds. For each (s,v)(s,v) such that 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)⊈𝒜\mathit{Cap}(s,v)\not\subseteq\mathcal{A}:

(15) ¬xs,v\neg x_{s,v}

The key novelty over classical package resolution is clause family (C5): it integrates the static capability analysis of Section 4 directly into the resolution process, ensuring that no installation plan can include a skill-version whose runtime requirements exceed the declared security policy.

Implementation.

We use the Glucose3 CDCL solver via the PySAT framework (Ignatiev et al., 2018). At-most-one constraints are encoded as pairwise negation (Eq. 11), which is compact for the typical case of |V⁡(s)|≤20|V(s)|\leq 20 versions per skill. For larger version spaces, sequential counter encodings from the PySAT cardinality module can be substituted.

6.4. Secure Installation

Definition 6.4 (Secure Installation).

An installation I⊆𝒮×ℕI\subseteq\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N} is a set of skill-version pairs. II is secure with respect to (𝒮,V,D,C,𝐶𝑎𝑝,𝒜)(\mathcal{S},V,D,C,\mathit{Cap},\mathcal{A}) if and only if:

  1. (1)

    Completeness. For every (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I and every (q,γ)∈D⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in D(s,v), there exists (q,w)∈I(q,w)\in I such that w⊧γw\models\gamma.

  2. (2)

    Consistency. For every (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I and every (q,γ)∈C⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in C(s,v), there is no (q,w)∈I(q,w)\in I with w⊧γw\models\gamma.

  3. (3)

    Capability safety. For every (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I: 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)⊆𝒜\mathit{Cap}(s,v)\subseteq\mathcal{A}.

Condition (3) is the agent-specific extension: it ties the installation plan to the capability-based sandboxing model of Section 5, ensuring that every installed skill respects the declared security boundary. In traditional package managers (apt, pip, npm), no analogue of this condition exists.

6.5. Lockfile Semantics

A lockfile is the deterministic serialization of a secure installation. We define the skill-lock.json format to provide three guarantees: reproducibility, integrity, and auditability.

Definition 6.5 (Lockfile).

A lockfile ℒ\mathcal{L} is a tuple ℒ=(I,H,M)\mathcal{L}=(I,H,M) where:

  • •

    I⊆𝒮×ℕI\subseteq\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N} is a secure installation (Definition 6.4).

  • •

    H:I→{0,1}256H\colon I\to\{0,1\}^{256} maps each installed skill-version to its SHA-256 content hash.

  • •

    MM is a metadata record containing the resolution strategy, the allowed capability set 𝒜\mathcal{A}, a generation timestamp, and the tool version.

Definition 6.6 (Lockfile Reproducibility).

A resolver ℛ\mathcal{R} is reproducible if, for any ADG and requirement set, running ℛ\mathcal{R} twice on the same input produces identical lockfiles:

ℛ⁡(𝐴𝐷𝐺,𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑠,𝒜)=ℛ⁡(𝐴𝐷𝐺,𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑠,𝒜)\mathcal{R}(\mathit{ADG},\mathit{reqs},\mathcal{A})=\mathcal{R}(\mathit{ADG},\mathit{reqs},\mathcal{A})

We achieve reproducibility by fixing the variable ordering in the SAT encoding (lexicographic by skill name, then descending version) and using a deterministic solver configuration. The lockfile itself is serialized with sorted keys and canonical JSON formatting, ensuring byte-identical output for identical inputs.

Definition 6.7 (Integrity Verification).

At installation time, for each (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I, the installer computes the SHA-256 hash of the skill content and verifies:

𝚜𝚑𝚊𝟸𝟻𝟼⁡(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s,v))=H⁡(s,v)\mathtt{sha256}(\mathit{content}(s,v))=H(s,v)

A mismatch indicates tampering: either the skill source was modified after resolution (supply chain attack), or the lockfile was corrupted.

This mechanism is analogous to the integrity fields in package-lock.json (npm) and Cargo.lock (Rust), adapted for the agent skill ecosystem where no prior lockfile standard exists.

6.6. Agent Skill Bill of Materials (ASBOM)

Regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act (Article 17, technical documentation requirements) (European Parliament, 2024) and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023) increasingly require transparency about third-party AI components. We generate an Agent Skill Bill of Materials (ASBOM) as a structured inventory of all skills in an agent’s dependency closure.

Definition 6.8 (Agent Skill Bill of Materials).

An ASBOM is a CycloneDX 1.6-compatible (OWASP, 2024b) document that records, for each (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I:

  • •

    Identity: skill name, version, format (Claude, MCP, OpenClaw), and content hash.

  • •

    Capabilities: the set 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)\mathit{Cap}(s,v) of declared runtime permissions.

  • •

    Dependencies: resolved dependency edges {(q,w)∣(q,γ)∈D(s,v),(q,w)∈I,w⊧γ}\{(q,w)\mid(q,\gamma)\in D(s,v),\;(q,w)\in I,\;w\models\gamma\}.

  • •

    Trust metadata: trust score, trust level (Section 7), and provenance information.

  • •

    Vulnerability status: known CVEs or analysis findings affecting (s,v)(s,v).

The CycloneDX format enables integration with existing enterprise vulnerability management platforms (e.g., Dependency-Track, Grype) and provides the machine-readable evidence required for compliance audits.

6.7. Transitive Vulnerability Propagation

A critical advantage of the graph-based model is the ability to propagate vulnerability information transitively.

Definition 6.9 (Affected Installation).

Given a set of known-vulnerable skill-versions 𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛⊆𝒮×ℕ\mathit{Vuln}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{N}, a skill-version (s,v)∈I∖𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛(s,v)\in I\setminus\mathit{Vuln} is transitively affected if there exists a path in the dependency graph from (s,v)(s,v) to some (q,w)∈𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛(q,w)\in\mathit{Vuln}. The set of affected installations is:

𝐴𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑(I,𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛)={(s,v)∈I∖𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛∣∃(q,w)∈𝑉𝑢𝑙𝑛.(s,v)↝∗(q,w)}\mathit{Affected}(I,\mathit{Vuln})=\{(s,v)\in I\setminus\mathit{Vuln}\mid\exists\,(q,w)\in\mathit{Vuln}\;.\;(s,v)\leadsto^{*}(q,w)\}

where ↝∗\leadsto^{*} denotes transitive reachability through dependency edges.

We compute 𝐴𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑\mathit{Affected} by BFS over the reverse dependency graph (from vulnerable nodes to their dependents), analogous to how npm audit identifies transitively affected packages. The difference is that our propagation also considers capability implications: if a vulnerable skill has capability c∈𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(q,w)c\in\mathit{Cap}(q,w), then all skills in its reverse transitive closure that delegate or depend on capability cc are flagged with elevated severity.

6.8. Theorem 4: Resolution Soundness

Theorem 6.10 (Resolution Soundness).

Let 𝐴𝐷𝐺=(𝒮,V,D,C,𝐶𝑎𝑝)\mathit{ADG}=(\mathcal{S},V,D,C,\mathit{Cap}) be an Agent Dependency Graph and 𝒜⊆𝒞\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C} a set of allowed capabilities. Let Φ\Phi be the conjunction of all clauses (C1)–(C5) from Definition 6.3. Then:

  1. (1)

    Φ\Phi is satisfiable if and only if a secure installation (Definition 6.4) exists.

  2. (2)

    Any satisfying assignment σ⊧Φ\sigma\models\Phi induces a secure installation Iσ={(s,v)∣σ⁡(xs,v)=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒}I_{\sigma}=\{(s,v)\mid\sigma(x_{s,v})=\mathit{true}\}, and the corresponding lockfile ℒσ=(Iσ,H,M)\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}=(I_{\sigma},H,M) satisfies all dependency, conflict, and capability constraints.

Proof sketch.

We establish both directions.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow)  Suppose σ⊧Φ\sigma\models\Phi. Define Iσ={(s,v)∣σ⁡(xs,v)=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒}I_{\sigma}=\{(s,v)\mid\sigma(x_{s,v})=\mathit{true}\}.

  • •

    At-most-one: By clause family (C1), for each skill ss at most one variable xs,vx_{s,v} is true, so IσI_{\sigma} contains at most one version per skill.

  • •

    Completeness: Fix (s,v)∈Iσ(s,v)\in I_{\sigma} and (q,γ)∈D⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in D(s,v). Since σ⁡(xs,v)=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒\sigma(x_{s,v})=\mathit{true}, clause (C3) requires σ⁡(xq,w)=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒\sigma(x_{q,w})=\mathit{true} for some w⊧γw\models\gamma. Hence (q,w)∈Iσ(q,w)\in I_{\sigma}.

  • •

    Consistency: Fix (s,v)∈Iσ(s,v)\in I_{\sigma} and (q,γ)∈C⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in C(s,v). For every w⊧γw\models\gamma, clause (C4) gives ¬xs,v∨¬xq,w\neg x_{s,v}\lor\neg x_{q,w}. Since σ⁡(xs,v)=𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒\sigma(x_{s,v})=\mathit{true}, we have σ⁡(xq,w)=𝑓𝑎𝑙𝑠𝑒\sigma(x_{q,w})=\mathit{false}, so (q,w)∉Iσ(q,w)\notin I_{\sigma}.

  • •

    Capability safety: If 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)⊈𝒜\mathit{Cap}(s,v)\not\subseteq\mathcal{A}, clause (C5) forces σ⁡(xs,v)=𝑓𝑎𝑙𝑠𝑒\sigma(x_{s,v})=\mathit{false}, so (s,v)∉Iσ(s,v)\notin I_{\sigma}. Contrapositive: (s,v)∈Iσ⇒𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)⊆𝒜(s,v)\in I_{\sigma}\Rightarrow\mathit{Cap}(s,v)\subseteq\mathcal{A}.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow)  Suppose II is a secure installation. Define σ(xs,v)=[(s,v)∈I]\sigma(x_{s,v})=[(s,v)\in I] (Iverson bracket).

  • •

    (C1): At most one version per skill in II (by definition of installation), so pairwise exclusion holds.

  • •

    (C2): For each requirement (s,γ)(s,\gamma), completeness of II implies some (s,w)∈I(s,w)\in I with w⊧γw\models\gamma, so the disjunction is satisfied.

  • •

    (C3): For each (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I and (q,γ)∈D⁡(s,v)(q,\gamma)\in D(s,v), completeness gives (q,w)∈I(q,w)\in I with w⊧γw\models\gamma, making the implication clause true. If (s,v)∉I(s,v)\notin I, the clause is trivially satisfied via ¬xs,v\neg x_{s,v}.

  • •

    (C4): Consistency of II ensures no conflicting pair is co-installed; the mutual exclusion clauses hold.

  • •

    (C5): Capability safety of II ensures 𝐶𝑎𝑝⁡(s,v)⊆𝒜\mathit{Cap}(s,v)\subseteq\mathcal{A} for all (s,v)∈I(s,v)\in I, so no unit clause ¬xs,v\neg x_{s,v} is violated.

Thus σ⊧Φ\sigma\models\Phi, and Φ\Phi is satisfiable. ∎

Remark 6.11.

The bidirectional correspondence in Theorem 6.10 means that the SAT solver provides a complete decision procedure for secure installability: if the solver reports UNSAT, then no secure installation exists under the given constraints. In such cases, the conflict analysis phase of the CDCL solver yields an unsatisfiable core, which we translate into human-readable diagnostic messages explaining which dependency, conflict, or capability constraint caused the failure.

Complexity.

The dependency resolution problem is NP-complete in general (Mancinelli et al., 2006). Our capability-bounded extension (clause family C5) adds only O⁡(|𝒮|⋅maxs⁡|V⁡(s)|)O(|\mathcal{S}|\cdot\max_{s}|V(s)|) unit clauses, so the theoretical worst case is unchanged. In practice, the agent skill ecosystem has |𝒮|≤103|\mathcal{S}|\leq 10^{3} and |V⁡(s)|≤20|V(s)|\leq 20, well within the efficient regime of modern CDCL solvers: our experiments (Section 9) show resolution times under 0.5 seconds for 500 skills.

Comparison with traditional package managers.

Table 3 summarizes the differences between our ADG-based resolver and traditional package dependency resolution.

7. Trust Score Algebra

The preceding sections established mechanisms for verifying individual skills (Sections 4–5) and resolving their dependencies securely (Section 6). A complementary question remains: how much should a developer trust a given skill? Binary safe/unsafe classification is insufficient in practice—skills exist on a spectrum from unsigned, anonymous submissions to formally verified, organization-signed artifacts with years of community track record.

This section introduces a trust score algebra that combines heterogeneous trust signals into a single composite score, propagates trust conservatively through dependency chains, models trust decay for unmaintained skills, and maps numeric scores to graduated assurance levels inspired by the SLSA framework (Google, 2023). Our construction draws on the trust management literature, particularly the PolicyMaker and KeyNote systems (Blaze et al., 1996; Blaze et al., 1999), and the formal trust models of Carbone et al. (Carbone et al., 2003) and Jøsang (Jøsang, 2001).

7.1. Trust Score Model

Definition 7.1 (Trust Signals).

For a skill ss at version vv, we define four orthogonal trust signals, each taking values in the closed interval [0,1][0,1]:

  1. (1)

    Tp​(s,v)∈[0,1]T_{p}(s,v)\in[0,1]: Provenance. Measures author verification and signing status. Tp=0T_{p}=0 for unsigned, anonymous authors; Tp=1T_{p}=1 for organization-signed skills with reproducible builds and verified identity.

  2. (2)

    Tb​(s,v)∈[0,1]T_{b}(s,v)\in[0,1]: Behavioral. Measures the outcome of static analysis (Section 4). Tb=0T_{b}=0 if critical capability violations are detected; Tb=1T_{b}=1 if analysis reports no findings.

  3. (3)

    Tc​(s,v)∈[0,1]T_{c}(s,v)\in[0,1]: Community. Aggregates community trust signals: usage count, age, issue reports, and peer reviews. Tc=0T_{c}=0 for a brand-new skill with no usage; Tc=1T_{c}=1 for a widely adopted, mature skill with no reported issues.

  4. (4)

    Th​(s,v)∈[0,1]T_{h}(s,v)\in[0,1]: Historical. Captures the skill’s past vulnerability record. Th=0T_{h}=0 if the skill has a history of CVEs or security incidents; Th=1T_{h}=1 for a clean historical record.

We write 𝐓⁡(s,v)=(Tp,Tb,Tc,Th)∈[0,1]4\mathbf{T}(s,v)=(T_{p},T_{b},T_{c},T_{h})\in[0,1]^{4} for the signal vector.

The four signals are designed to be orthogonal: provenance measures who published the skill, behavioral measures what the skill does, community measures how widely it is adopted, and historical measures how reliable it has been over time.

Definition 7.2 (Trust Weights).

A weight vector 𝐰=(wp,wb,wc,wh)∈ℝ≥04\mathbf{w}=(w_{p},w_{b},w_{c},w_{h})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{4} satisfies:

wp+wb+wc+wh=1andwp,wb,wc,wh≥0w_{p}+w_{b}+w_{c}+w_{h}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad w_{p},w_{b},w_{c},w_{h}\geq 0

The default weight vector is 𝐰0=(0.3,0.3,0.2,0.2)\mathbf{w}_{0}=(0.3,0.3,0.2,0.2), reflecting equal priority for provenance and behavioral analysis (the signals most directly under the tool’s and author’s control), with lower weight for community and historical signals (which accumulate over time).

Definition 7.3 (Intrinsic Trust Score).

The intrinsic trust score of skill ss at version vv is the weighted linear combination:

(16) T⁡(s,v)=wp⋅Tp​(s,v)+wb⋅Tb​(s,v)+wc⋅Tc​(s,v)+wh⋅Th​(s,v)T(s,v)=w_{p}\cdot T_{p}(s,v)+w_{b}\cdot T_{b}(s,v)+w_{c}\cdot T_{c}(s,v)+w_{h}\cdot T_{h}(s,v)

Since all weights are non-negative and sum to 11, and all signals are in [0,1][0,1], the score satisfies T⁡(s,v)∈[0,1]T(s,v)\in[0,1].
