Appendix A Full Proofs

This appendix provides complete, rigorous proofs for all five theorems stated in the main text. We restate each theorem for self-containedness before presenting the proof.

A.1. Theorem 3.6: DY-Skill Maximality

Definition A.1 (DY-Skill Adversary, restated).

A DY-Skill adversary 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} is a probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) machine that controls the communication channel between the agent runtime ℛ\mathcal{R} and the skill execution environment ℰ\mathcal{E}. The adversary has the following capabilities:

  1. (i)

    Intercept: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can observe any message mm sent between ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℰ\mathcal{E}.

  2. (ii)

    Inject: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can inject arbitrary messages m′m^{\prime} into the channel.

  3. (iii)

    Modify: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can replace any message mm with m′≠mm^{\prime}\neq m.

  4. (iv)

    Drop: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can suppress any message.

  5. (v)

    Forge skills: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can create skill definitions s′s^{\prime} with arbitrary content, including:

    • •

      Skill manifest with arbitrary capability declarations CdeclaredC_{\text{declared}}

    • •

      Executable code implementing capabilities Cactual⊇CdeclaredC_{\text{actual}}\supseteq C_{\text{declared}}

    • •

      Metadata mimicking legitimate skills (name squatting, version manipulation)

  6. (vi)

    Compromise registries: 𝒜\mathcal{A} can modify skill entries in the registry 𝒫\mathcal{P}, subject to the constraint that 𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot forge valid cryptographic signatures under keys it does not possess.

Definition A.2 (Classical Dolev-Yao Adversary).

A classical Dolev-Yao adversary 𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}} operates over a network protocol Π\Pi with capabilities (i)–(iv) from the definition above, applied to protocol messages. 𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}} additionally possesses the standard Dolev-Yao deduction rules for message construction and decomposition.

Definition A.3 (Simulation).

Adversary 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} simulates adversary 𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{2} (written 𝒜1⪰𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{1}\succeq\mathcal{A}_{2}) if for every attack strategy σ2\sigma_{2} of 𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{2}, there exists a strategy σ1\sigma_{1} of 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} such that the observable effects on the system are computationally indistinguishable:

∀σ2∈Strat(𝒜2),∃σ1∈Strat(𝒜1):Viewℛ(σ1)≈cViewℛ(σ2)\forall\sigma_{2}\in\textit{Strat}(\mathcal{A}_{2}),\;\exists\sigma_{1}\in\textit{Strat}(\mathcal{A}_{1})\colon\;\textit{View}_{\mathcal{R}}(\sigma_{1})\approx_{c}\textit{View}_{\mathcal{R}}(\sigma_{2})

where Viewℛ​(σ)\textit{View}_{\mathcal{R}}(\sigma) denotes the distribution of observations by the runtime ℛ\mathcal{R} under strategy σ\sigma, and ≈c\approx_{c} denotes computational indistinguishability.

Theorem A.4 (DY-Skill Maximality, restated).

𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} is maximal among PPT skill adversaries: for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} operating on agent skill channels, 𝒜DY-Skill⪰𝒜\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}\succeq\mathcal{A}. Moreover, 𝒜DY-Skill⪰𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}\succeq\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}} when the DY-Skill channel is instantiated as a standard network protocol.

Proof.

We prove the two claims separately.

Claim 1: Maximality over skill adversaries.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any PPT adversary operating on agent skill channels. We construct a simulation strategy σDY-Skill\sigma_{\textit{DY-Skill}} for 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} that reproduces any strategy σ𝒜\sigma_{\mathcal{A}} of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Any action by 𝒜\mathcal{A} on the skill channel falls into exactly one of the following categories:

  1. (a)

    Channel manipulation (intercept, inject, modify, drop): These are capabilities (i)–(iv) of 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}. The simulation is the identity: 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} performs the same channel operation.

  2. (b)

    Skill forgery (creating a malicious skill definition): This is capability (v). Since 𝒜\mathcal{A} is PPT, the forged skill s′s^{\prime} can be computed in polynomial time. 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} computes the same s′s^{\prime} using capability (v) and injects it using capability (ii).

  3. (c)

    Registry manipulation (modifying skill entries): This is capability (vi). 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} applies the same registry modifications, subject to the identical cryptographic constraint.

  4. (d)

    Computation on observed data (e.g., analyzing intercepted messages to craft adaptive attacks): Since both 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} are PPT, any polynomial-time computation that 𝒜\mathcal{A} performs on observed data can also be performed by 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}.

Since every action category of 𝒜\mathcal{A} maps to a capability of 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}, the simulation is complete. For any strategy σ𝒜\sigma_{\mathcal{A}}:

Viewℛ​(σDY-Skill)=Viewℛ​(σ𝒜)\textit{View}_{\mathcal{R}}(\sigma_{\textit{DY-Skill}})=\textit{View}_{\mathcal{R}}(\sigma_{\mathcal{A}})

with equality (not merely computational indistinguishability), since the simulation is exact.

Claim 2: Subsumption of classical DY.

Let σDY\sigma_{\textit{DY}} be any strategy of 𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}} over a protocol Π\Pi. We instantiate the DY-Skill channel as the protocol channel of Π\Pi.

Capabilities (i)–(iv) of 𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}} map directly to capabilities (i)–(iv) of 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}. The Dolev-Yao deduction rules (pairing, projection, encryption, decryption with known keys) are polynomial-time operations, hence executable by the PPT 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}.

Capabilities (v) and (vi) of 𝒜DY-Skill\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}} are additional capabilities not present in 𝒜DY\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}}. Therefore, Strat​(𝒜DY)⊆Strat​(𝒜DY-Skill)\textit{Strat}(\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY}})\subseteq\textit{Strat}(\mathcal{A}_{\textit{DY-Skill}}), and the simulation is the identity embedding. ∎

A.2. Theorem 4.9: Analysis Soundness

We prove soundness directly over the capability domain 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|} defined in Section 4.1, which is the domain on which the main-text theorem is stated.

Theorem A.5 (Analysis Soundness, restated).

Let ss be a skill with declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s). If the abstract analysis over the capability domain 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|} reports no violations—i.e., 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset—then for every concrete execution trace τ\tau of ss and every resource access (r,ℓ)(r,\ell) performed in τ\tau:

ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r).
Proof.

We prove the soundness condition α∘⟦s⟧⊑⟦s⟧♯∘α\alpha\circ\llbracket s\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\alpha (Proposition 4.7) by verifying that each concrete transfer function from Section 4.3 is soundly over-approximated by the corresponding abstract transfer function in the capability domain. The proof proceeds in two parts: (1) verifying soundness of each per-resource transfer function, and (2) lifting to composite constructs by structural induction.

Part 1: Transfer function soundness (per resource type).

For each resource type r∈𝒞r\in\mathcal{C}, we verify that the abstract transfer function τr♯\tau_{r}^{\sharp} over-approximates the concrete capability footprint. Let αr​(S)∈𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\alpha_{r}(S)\in\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}} be the abstraction of a set of concrete states SS projected onto resource rr: the least access level ℓ\ell such that every state in SS accesses rr at level ℓ\ell or below. We verify αr​(S)⊑τr♯​(αr​(S))\alpha_{r}(S)\sqsubseteq\tau_{r}^{\sharp}(\alpha_{r}(S)) for each transfer function:

  1. (1)

    Network (URL reference). Pattern: URL string detected in skill content. Concrete: The skill may issue HTTP GET requests, accessing network at level 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}. Abstract: τnetwork♯:=𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\tau_{\texttt{network}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{READ}. Soundness: αnetwork​(S)∈{𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣}⊑𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣=τnetwork♯\alpha_{\texttt{network}}(S)\in\{\mathsf{NONE},\mathsf{READ}\}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{READ}=\tau_{\texttt{network}}^{\sharp}. ✓

  2. (2)

    Network (HTTP write method). Pattern: POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE detected. Concrete: The skill may issue mutating HTTP requests, accessing network at level 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}. Abstract: τnetwork♯:=𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\tau_{\texttt{network}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{WRITE}. Soundness: Any concrete access is at most 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤⊑𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{WRITE}. ✓

  3. (3)

    Shell (command invocation). Pattern: Shell command invocation detected. Concrete: The skill may execute arbitrary shell commands, accessing shell at level 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}. Abstract: τshell♯:=𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\tau_{\texttt{shell}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{WRITE}. Soundness: Concrete shell access is at most 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}. The abstract result matches. ✓

  4. (4)

    Environment (variable reference). Pattern: Environment variable reference detected. Concrete: The skill reads environment variables, accessing environment at level 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}. Abstract: τenvironment♯:=𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\tau_{\texttt{environment}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{READ}. Soundness: Reading an environment variable is at most 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣⊑𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{READ}. ✓

  5. (5)

    Filesystem (read operation). Pattern: File read keyword detected. Concrete: The skill reads files, accessing filesystem at level 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}. Abstract: τfilesystem♯:=𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\tau_{\texttt{filesystem}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{READ}. Soundness: 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣⊑𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{READ}. ✓

  6. (6)

    Filesystem (write operation). Pattern: File write keyword detected. Concrete: The skill writes files, accessing filesystem at level 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}. Abstract: τfilesystem♯:=𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\tau_{\texttt{filesystem}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{WRITE}. Soundness: 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤⊑𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{WRITE}. ✓

  7. (7)

    Skill invocation. Pattern: Sub-skill invocation detected. Concrete: The skill invokes another skill, accessing skill_invoke at level 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ} (query) or 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE} (mutation). Abstract: τskill_invoke♯:=𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\tau_{\texttt{skill\_invoke}}^{\sharp}:=\mathsf{WRITE} (conservative over-approximation). Soundness: Any concrete invocation is at most 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤⊑𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE}\sqsubseteq\mathsf{WRITE}. ✓

  8. (8)

    Remaining resources (clipboard, browser, database). Transfer functions follow the same pattern: keyword presence maps to 𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣\mathsf{READ} or 𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤\mathsf{WRITE} depending on the detected operation type. Each concrete access is bounded by the abstract inference. ✓

In all cases, the abstract transfer function assigns a capability level ℓ♯\ell^{\sharp} such that αr​(S)⊑ℓ♯\alpha_{r}(S)\sqsubseteq\ell^{\sharp} for every concrete state set SS matching the detected pattern. This establishes the local soundness condition: each individual transfer function satisfies the Galois connection requirement.

Part 2: Structural induction over composite constructs.

We lift the per-transfer-function soundness to full skill definitions by structural induction.

Case: Sequential composition (s1;s2s_{1};\,s_{2}). By the induction hypothesis, both ⟦s1⟧♯\llbracket s_{1}\rrbracket^{\sharp} and ⟦s2⟧♯\llbracket s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp} are sound. The composed abstract semantics is ⟦s1;s2⟧♯=⟦s2⟧♯∘⟦s1⟧♯\llbracket s_{1};\,s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp}=\llbracket s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\llbracket s_{1}\rrbracket^{\sharp}. By monotonicity of both abstract functions and the standard composition lemma for Galois connections (Cousot and Cousot, 1977):

α∘⟦s1;s2⟧⊑⟦s2⟧♯∘⟦s1⟧♯∘α=⟦s1;s2⟧♯∘α.\alpha\circ\llbracket s_{1};\,s_{2}\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\llbracket s_{1}\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\alpha=\llbracket s_{1};\,s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\alpha.

Case: Conditional (if​b​then​s1​else​s2\texttt{if}~b~\texttt{then}~s_{1}~\texttt{else}~s_{2}). Concretely, exactly one branch executes. Abstractly, we take the pointwise join: ⟦if⋯⟧♯(a)=⟦s1⟧♯(a)⊔⟦s2⟧♯(a)\llbracket\texttt{if}~\cdots\rrbracket^{\sharp}(a)=\llbracket s_{1}\rrbracket^{\sharp}(a)\sqcup\llbracket s_{2}\rrbracket^{\sharp}(a). Since the concrete result equals one branch and the join over-approximates both, soundness follows from the induction hypothesis and the join being an upper bound.

Case: Loop (while​b​do​sbody\texttt{while}~b~\texttt{do}~s_{\text{body}}). The abstract semantics computes the least fixpoint of λ​a.a0⊔⟦sbody⟧♯​(a)\lambda a.\;a_{0}\sqcup\llbracket s_{\text{body}}\rrbracket^{\sharp}(a). By Tarski’s fixpoint theorem and the fact that 𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝|𝒞|\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}^{|\mathcal{C}|} has finite height 48=65,5364^{8}=65{,}536, the ascending chain stabilizes. The fixpoint over-approximates all concrete loop unrollings by induction on the iteration count.

Conclusion. By structural induction, α∘⟦s⟧⊑⟦s⟧♯∘α\alpha\circ\llbracket s\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket s\rrbracket^{\sharp}\circ\alpha for all skill definitions ss. Combined with the violation check (𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅⇒𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset\Rightarrow\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)), we obtain the theorem: every concrete resource access (r,ℓ)(r,\ell) satisfies ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r). ∎

A.3. Theorem 5.6: Static Capability Confinement

Definition A.6 (Operation Capability Mapping).

Each operation oo in a skill’s code has a capability requirement 𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)=(r,ℓ)∈𝒞×𝕃𝑐𝑎𝑝\mathit{cap}(o)=(r,\ell)\in\mathcal{C}\times\mathbb{L}_{\mathit{cap}}, mapping it to a resource type and minimum access level:

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(read_file)=(filesystem,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{read\_file})=(\texttt{filesystem},\mathsf{READ})

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(write_file)=(filesystem,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{write\_file})=(\texttt{filesystem},\mathsf{WRITE})

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(read_env)=(environment,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{read\_env})=(\texttt{environment},\mathsf{READ})

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(exec)=(shell,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{exec})=(\texttt{shell},\mathsf{WRITE})

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(http_get)=(network,𝖱𝖤𝖠𝖣)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{http\_get})=(\texttt{network},\mathsf{READ})

  • •

    𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(http_post)=(network,𝖶𝖱𝖨𝖳𝖤)\mathit{cap}(\texttt{http\_post})=(\texttt{network},\mathsf{WRITE})

The set of all operations syntactically present in skill ss is 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)\mathit{ops}(s). The inferred capability set is defined resource-wise:

𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)=⨆o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o).r=r𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o).ℓ\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}o\in\mathit{ops}(s)\\ \mathit{cap}(o).r=r\end{subarray}}\mathit{cap}(o).\ell

with 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)=𝖭𝖮𝖭𝖤\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)=\mathsf{NONE} if no operation accesses resource rr.

Theorem A.7 (Static Capability Confinement, restated).

Let ss be a skill with declared capability set 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s). If 𝑉𝑖𝑜𝑙⁡(s)=∅\mathit{Viol}(s)=\emptyset (i.e., 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)), then for every operation oo syntactically reachable in ss:

𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D(s)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r).\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(\mathit{cap}(o).r).
Proof.

By structural induction on the syntax of skill code. The key invariant is: for every code construct s′s^{\prime} in the skill, every operation o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s′)o\in\mathit{ops}(s^{\prime}) satisfies 𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I(s)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r)\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(\mathit{cap}(o).r). Combined with the hypothesis 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s), this yields the theorem by transitivity.

Base case: Single operation oo.

The skill consists of a single operation oo with 𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o)=(r,ℓ)\mathit{cap}(o)=(r,\ell). By definition of 𝐶𝑎𝑝I\mathit{Cap}_{I}:

ℓ=𝑐𝑎𝑝⁡(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)\ell=\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)

since o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)o\in\mathit{ops}(s) and 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r) is defined as the join over all such operations. By hypothesis 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r), so ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)​(r)\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(r) by transitivity.

Inductive case: Sequential composition (s1;s2s_{1};\,s_{2}).

We have 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s1,s2)=𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s1)∪𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s2)\mathit{ops}(s_{1};\,s_{2})=\mathit{ops}(s_{1})\cup\mathit{ops}(s_{2}). By the induction hypothesis, every operation in 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s1)\mathit{ops}(s_{1}) and 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s2)\mathit{ops}(s_{2}) individually satisfies the bound. Since 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s1,s2)​(r)=𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s1)​(r)⊔𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s2)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{1};\,s_{2})(r)=\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{1})(r)\sqcup\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{2})(r) and the join is the least upper bound, every individual operation capability is below the join:

∀o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠(s1;s2):𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I(s1;s2)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D(s)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r).\forall\,o\in\mathit{ops}(s_{1};\,s_{2})\colon\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{1};\,s_{2})(\mathit{cap}(o).r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(\mathit{cap}(o).r).

Inductive case: Conditional (if​b​then​s1​else​s2\texttt{if}~b~\texttt{then}~s_{1}~\texttt{else}~s_{2}).

The analysis conservatively includes both branches: 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)=𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s1)∪𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s2)\mathit{ops}(s)=\mathit{ops}(s_{1})\cup\mathit{ops}(s_{2}). At runtime, only one branch executes. If branch sis_{i} executes, each operation o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(si)o\in\mathit{ops}(s_{i}) satisfies 𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I(si)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r)\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{i})(\mathit{cap}(o).r) by the induction hypothesis. Since 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(si)⊆𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)\mathit{ops}(s_{i})\subseteq\mathit{ops}(s), we have 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(si)​(r)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)​(r)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s_{i})(r)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)(r) for all rr, and hence 𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D(s)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r)\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(\mathit{cap}(o).r) by transitivity through 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s).

Inductive case: Loop (while​b​do​sbody\texttt{while}~b~\texttt{do}~s_{\text{body}}).

The set of operations is 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(while​b​do​sbody)=𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(sbody)\mathit{ops}(\texttt{while}~b~\texttt{do}~s_{\text{body}})=\mathit{ops}(s_{\text{body}}), since the loop body is the only code that executes (repetition does not introduce new syntactic operations). By the induction hypothesis on sbodys_{\text{body}}, every o∈𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(sbody)o\in\mathit{ops}(s_{\text{body}}) satisfies the bound. Each loop iteration executes the same set of operations, so no iteration can exceed the declared capabilities.

Inductive case: Function call (f⁡(x1,…,xk)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})).

If ff is a built-in operation, it falls under the base case. If ff is a user-defined function, its body is a sub-skill with 𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(f)⊆𝑜𝑝𝑠⁡(s)\mathit{ops}(f)\subseteq\mathit{ops}(s) (since ff’s body is part of the analyzed skill). By the induction hypothesis on ff’s body, all operations satisfy the bound.

Conclusion. By structural induction, every operation oo syntactically reachable during any execution of ss satisfies 𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).ℓ⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D(s)(𝑐𝑎𝑝(o).r)\mathit{cap}(o).\ell\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)(\mathit{cap}(o).r). The proof relies only on the definition of 𝐶𝑎𝑝I\mathit{Cap}_{I} (the pointwise join over operation capabilities) and the hypothesis 𝐶𝑎𝑝I​(s)⊑𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{I}(s)\sqsubseteq\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s)—it does not assume any runtime sandbox mechanism. ∎

Runtime Confinement (Design Theorem). Theorem 5.7 follows from the object-capability confinement result of Maffeis et al. (2010): in a capability-safe execution environment where (a) there is no ambient authority, (b) capabilities are unforgeable, and (c) the sandbox mediates every action via Equation (7), the only capabilities available to ss are those in 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s). Since 𝐶𝑎𝑝D​(s)\mathit{Cap}_{D}(s) is the initial endowment and the four Dennis–Van Horn mechanisms (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966) can only attenuate (never amplify) authority (Proposition 5.5), the runtime check in Equation (7) suffices to guarantee Equation (10). The formal details follow the proof structure of Maffeis et al. (2010, Theorem 4.1), instantiated for the agent skill capability model of Section 5.1.

A.4. Theorem 6.10: Resolution Soundness

Definition A.8 (SAT Encoding).

The SAT encoding of an ADG 𝒢\mathcal{G} introduces:

  • •

    Boolean variable xs,vx_{s,v} for each skill s∈Vs\in V and version v∈versions​(s)v\in\textit{versions}(s), where xs,v=⊤x_{s,v}=\top means version vv of skill ss is selected.

  • •

    At-most-one clause for each skill: ⋀v≠v′(¬xs,v∨¬xs,v′)\bigwedge_{v\neq v^{\prime}}(\neg x_{s,v}\lor\neg x_{s,v^{\prime}}).

  • •

    At-least-one clause for each skill: ⋁v∈versions​(s)xs,v\bigvee_{v\in\textit{versions}(s)}x_{s,v}.

  • •

    Dependency constraint for each edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E with constraint μ⁡(u,v)\mu(u,v): if xu,vu=⊤x_{u,v_{u}}=\top, then exactly one xv,vvx_{v,v_{v}} with vv∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))v_{v}\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)) must be true.

where sat​(c)\textit{sat}(c) denotes the set of versions satisfying constraint cc.

Definition A.9 (Valid Resolution).

A valid resolution of an ADG 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a function r:V→Versionr\colon V\to\textit{Version} such that:

  1. (i)

    ∀s∈V:r⁡(s)∈versions​(s)\forall s\in V\colon r(s)\in\textit{versions}(s) (version exists)

  2. (ii)

    ∀(u,v)∈E:r⁡(v)∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))\forall(u,v)\in E\colon r(v)\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)) (constraints satisfied)

  3. (iii)

    The graph (V,E)(V,E) is acyclic (no circular dependencies)

Theorem A.10 (Resolution Soundness, restated).

The SAT encoding is equisatisfiable with the dependency resolution problem: the SAT formula is satisfiable if and only if a valid resolution exists. Moreover, any satisfying assignment σ\sigma of the SAT formula yields a valid resolution rσr_{\sigma}, and any valid resolution rr yields a satisfying assignment σr\sigma_{r}.

Proof.

We prove both directions of the bijection.

Direction 1: Satisfying assignment ⇒\Rightarrow valid resolution.

Let σ\sigma be a satisfying assignment of the SAT formula. Define rσ​(s)=vr_{\sigma}(s)=v where σ(xs,v)=⊤\sigma(x_{s,v})=\top.

Well-definedness: By the at-least-one clause, at least one xs,vx_{s,v} is true for each ss. By the at-most-one clause, at most one is true. Hence exactly one version is selected: rσr_{\sigma} is a well-defined function.

Condition (i): Since xs,vx_{s,v} only exists for v∈versions​(s)v\in\textit{versions}(s), we have rσ​(s)∈versions​(s)r_{\sigma}(s)\in\textit{versions}(s).

Condition (ii): Let (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E with rσ​(u)=vur_{\sigma}(u)=v_{u}. The dependency constraint clause states: xu,vu⇒⋁vv∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))xv,vvx_{u,v_{u}}\Rightarrow\bigvee_{v_{v}\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v))}x_{v,v_{v}}. Since σ(xu,vu)=⊤\sigma(x_{u,v_{u}})=\top and σ\sigma satisfies this clause, there exists vv∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))v_{v}\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)) with σ(xv,vv)=⊤\sigma(x_{v,v_{v}})=\top. By the at-most-one clause, rσ​(v)=vv∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))r_{\sigma}(v)=v_{v}\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)).

Condition (iii): Cycle detection is performed as a preprocessing step (Kahn’s algorithm) before SAT encoding. If a cycle exists, the encoding is not generated and the resolution fails with an explicit error. Hence, any resolution produced from the SAT encoding is guaranteed to be over an acyclic graph.

Direction 2: Valid resolution ⇒\Rightarrow satisfying assignment.

Let rr be a valid resolution. Define σr(xs,v)=⊤\sigma_{r}(x_{s,v})=\top iff r⁡(s)=vr(s)=v, and σr(xs,v)=⊥\sigma_{r}(x_{s,v})=\bot otherwise.

At-most-one: For each skill ss, exactly one version r⁡(s)r(s) is selected, so exactly one xs,vx_{s,v} is true.

At-least-one: Since r⁡(s)r(s) is defined for all s∈Vs\in V, at least one xs,vx_{s,v} is true.

Dependency constraints: For each (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E with r⁡(u)=vur(u)=v_{u}: σr(xu,vu)=⊤\sigma_{r}(x_{u,v_{u}})=\top, and by condition (ii) of valid resolution, r​(v)∈sat​(μ​(u,v))r(v)\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)). Let vv=r⁡(v)v_{v}=r(v); then σr(xv,vv)=⊤\sigma_{r}(x_{v,v_{v}})=\top and vv∈sat​(μ⁡(u,v))v_{v}\in\textit{sat}(\mu(u,v)). The dependency clause is satisfied.

Bijection. The mappings σ↦rσ\sigma\mapsto r_{\sigma} and r↦σrr\mapsto\sigma_{r} are inverses:

  • •

    rσr​(s)=vr_{\sigma_{r}}(s)=v where σr(xs,v)=⊤\sigma_{r}(x_{s,v})=\top, i.e., where r⁡(s)=vr(s)=v. So rσr=rr_{\sigma_{r}}=r.

  • •

    σrσ(xs,v)=⊤\sigma_{r_{\sigma}}(x_{s,v})=\top iff rσ​(s)=vr_{\sigma}(s)=v iff σ(xs,v)=⊤\sigma(x_{s,v})=\top. So σrσ=σ\sigma_{r_{\sigma}}=\sigma.

Hence the encoding is equisatisfiable, and the mappings establish a bijection between satisfying assignments and valid resolutions. ∎

A.5. Theorem 7.12: Trust Monotonicity

Definition A.11 (Trust Score, restated).

The trust score of a skill ss at time tt is:

τ⁡(s,t)=∑i=1kwi⋅σi​(s,t)\tau(s,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\sigma_{i}(s,t)

where:

  • •

    kk is the number of trust signals.

  • •

    𝐰=(w1,…,wk)∈Δk−1\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{k})\in\Delta^{k-1} is a weight vector in the probability simplex (wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0, ∑iwi=1\sum_{i}w_{i}=1).

  • •

    σi​(s,t)∈[0,1]\sigma_{i}(s,t)\in[0,1] is the value of trust signal ii for skill ss at time tt.

Definition A.12 (Signal Update).

A signal update at time t+1t{+}1 is a vector δ=(δ1,…,δk)\delta=(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{k}) where:

σi​(s,t+1)=clamp​(σi​(s,t)+δi, 0, 1)\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)=\textit{clamp}(\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i},\;0,\;1)

An update is non-negative if δi≥0\delta_{i}\geq 0 for all i∈{1,…,k}i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.

Theorem A.13 (Trust Monotonicity, restated).

If all signal updates between time tt and t+1t{+}1 are non-negative (i.e., δi≥0\delta_{i}\geq 0 for all ii) and no temporal decay is applied (di​(t)=1d_{i}(t)=1 for all i,ti,t), then:

τ⁡(s,t+1)≥τ⁡(s,t)\tau(s,t{+}1)\geq\tau(s,t)
Proof.

We proceed by direct computation.

Step 1: Express the difference.

τ⁡(s,t+1)−τ⁡(s,t)\displaystyle\tau(s,t{+}1)-\tau(s,t) =∑i=1kwi⋅σi​(s,t+1)−∑i=1kwi⋅σi​(s,t)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\sigma_{i}(s,t)
=∑i=1kwi⋅(σi​(s,t+1)−σi​(s,t))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\bigl(\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sigma_{i}(s,t)\bigr)

Step 2: Bound each signal difference.

For each signal ii, we have:

σi​(s,t+1)=clamp​(σi​(s,t)+δi, 0, 1)\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)=\textit{clamp}(\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i},\;0,\;1)

Since δi≥0\delta_{i}\geq 0:

σi​(s,t)+δi≥σi​(s,t)\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i}\geq\sigma_{i}(s,t)

The clamp function clamp​(x,0,1)=max⁡(0,min⁡(1,x))\textit{clamp}(x,0,1)=\max(0,\min(1,x)) is monotone non-decreasing in xx:

  • •

    If σi​(s,t)+δi≤1\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i}\leq 1: σi​(s,t+1)=σi​(s,t)+δi≥σi​(s,t)\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)=\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i}\geq\sigma_{i}(s,t).

  • •

    If σi​(s,t)+δi>1\sigma_{i}(s,t)+\delta_{i}>1: σi​(s,t+1)=1≥σi​(s,t)\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)=1\geq\sigma_{i}(s,t) (since σi​(s,t)≤1\sigma_{i}(s,t)\leq 1).

In both cases:

σi​(s,t+1)−σi​(s,t)≥0\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sigma_{i}(s,t)\geq 0

Step 3: Combine with non-negative weights.

Since wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0 (from the simplex constraint) and σi​(s,t+1)−σi​(s,t)≥0\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sigma_{i}(s,t)\geq 0 (from Step 2):

wi⋅(σi​(s,t+1)−σi​(s,t))≥0for all ​iw_{i}\cdot\bigl(\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sigma_{i}(s,t)\bigr)\geq 0\quad\text{for all }i

Therefore:

τ⁡(s,t+1)−τ⁡(s,t)=∑i=1kwi⋅(σi​(s,t+1)−σi​(s,t))≥0\tau(s,t{+}1)-\tau(s,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\bigl(\sigma_{i}(s,t{+}1)-\sigma_{i}(s,t)\bigr)\geq 0

Step 4: Boundedness.

We additionally verify that τ⁡(s,t)∈[0,1]\tau(s,t)\in[0,1] for all s,ts,t:

Lower bound: Since wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0 and σi​(s,t)≥0\sigma_{i}(s,t)\geq 0 (by the clamp lower bound):

τ⁡(s,t)=∑i=1kwi⋅σi​(s,t)≥0\tau(s,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\sigma_{i}(s,t)\geq 0

Upper bound: Since σi​(s,t)≤1\sigma_{i}(s,t)\leq 1 (by the clamp upper bound) and ∑iwi=1\sum_{i}w_{i}=1:

τ⁡(s,t)=∑i=1kwi⋅σi​(s,t)≤∑i=1kwi⋅1=1\tau(s,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot\sigma_{i}(s,t)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}w_{i}\cdot 1=1

Conclusion. τ⁡(s,t+1)≥τ⁡(s,t)\tau(s,t{+}1)\geq\tau(s,t) whenever all signal updates are non-negative and no temporal decay is applied. Furthermore, τ⁡(s,t)∈[0,1]\tau(s,t)\in[0,1] for all ss and tt. ∎

Remark A.14 (Effect of Temporal Decay).

When temporal decay is active (di​(t)<1d_{i}(t)<1 for some ii), the monotonicity property may not hold in general, since the decay factor can reduce trust even in the absence of negative evidence. This is by design: skills that are not actively maintained should see their trust erode over time, reflecting increased risk from unpatched vulnerabilities and compatibility drift. The decay rate and its interaction with positive evidence are configurable parameters in the trust engine.

Appendix B SkillFortifyBench Details

This appendix provides the full specification of SkillFortifyBench, including the attack type distribution across formats, example skills, and the labeling methodology.

B.1. Attack Type Distribution

Table 11 shows the complete distribution of attack types across the three skill formats. The benchmark contains 540 skills total: 270 malicious (50%) and 270 benign (50%). Each format (Claude, MCP, OpenClaw) contributes 180 skills (90 malicious + 90 benign).

B.2. Example Skills

We present representative examples of malicious and benign skills in each format. All examples are simplified for exposition; full skills in SkillFortifyBench contain additional realistic metadata.

B.2.1. Malicious Claude Code Skill (A1 — Data Exfiltration via HTTP)

SkillFortify detects this skill through two findings: (1) pattern match on os.environ combined with requests.post to an external URL (A1 pattern), and (2) information flow analysis tracing data from the env source through env_data to the net sink at requests.post.

B.2.2. Malicious MCP Server Configuration (A4 — Arbitrary Code Execution)

SkillFortify detects the subprocess.Popen with shell invocation piped through curl, matching the A4 arbitrary code execution pattern. The command passes inline Python via -c, a pattern commonly observed in ClawHavoc (Zhang et al., 2026) payloads.

B.2.3. Benign OpenClaw Skill

This skill declares only read_local permission, consistent with its stated purpose. SkillFortify correctly classifies it as benign: no malicious patterns match, no information flow violations are detected, and the inferred capabilities ({ReadLocal}\{\textsc{ReadLocal}\}) are confined within declared capabilities.

B.3. Labeling Methodology

SkillFortifyBench uses constructive ground truth: skills are generated by a deterministic benchmark generator that embeds specific, known attack patterns into malicious skills and generates clean implementations for benign skills. This approach has three advantages over post-hoc labeling:

  1. (1)

    Perfect ground truth. Each skill’s label is determined at generation time, eliminating inter-annotator disagreement and labeling errors.

  2. (2)

    Reproducibility. The generator uses seeded pseudo-random number generators (Python random.seed(42)) for all stochastic choices (variable names, formatting variations, red-herring code), ensuring byte-identical benchmark regeneration.

  3. (3)

    Controlled complexity. Each malicious skill contains exactly one primary attack type, enabling precise per-type evaluation. Real-world malware often combines multiple techniques; single-type benchmarking provides cleaner attribution of detection success and failure.

Attack pattern sources.

The 13 attack types are derived from three verified sources:

  • •

    ClawHavoc campaign (arXiv:2602.20867, Feb 24, 2026) (Zhang et al., 2026): 1,200+ malicious skills documented with 7 skill design patterns. Contributes patterns for A1–A6 and A13.

  • •

    MalTool dataset (arXiv:2602.12194, Feb 12, 2026) (Wang et al., 2026b): 6,487 malicious tools catalogued. Contributes patterns for A7–A10.

  • •

    CVE-2026-25253 advisory (Ethiack, 2026): Remote code execution via skill installation. Contributes the A4 variant specific to the exploitation vector.

  • •

    Literature survey (“Agent Skills in the Wild,” arXiv:2601.10338) (Park et al., 2026): 14 vulnerability patterns across 42,447 skills. Contributes patterns for A11 and A12. Corroborated by a second large-scale study scanning 98,380 skills with 157 confirmed malicious entries (Li et al., 2026).

Benign skill sources.

Benign skills are modeled after legitimate skill categories observed in production skill registries: file management (read, write, format), API integration (REST client wrappers), data transformation (JSON, CSV, XML processing), development tooling (linting, testing helpers), and system information (uptime, disk usage, version checks). Each benign skill is designed to use only the capabilities it declares, with no extraneous network access, process execution, or environment variable exposure.

Appendix C Lockfile Schema

This appendix specifies the complete skill-lock.json schema, field descriptions, and an example lockfile produced by skillfortify lock.

C.1. Schema Specification

The lockfile is a JSON document conforming to the following schema. We present it in JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) notation.

C.2. Field Descriptions

Table 12 provides detailed descriptions of all top-level and nested fields.

C.3. Example Lockfile

Listing  shows an example skill-lock.json for a three-skill agent configuration.

Key properties of the example.

The lockfile demonstrates several features of the schema:

  1. (1)

    Deterministic ordering. Skills are sorted alphabetically by name (api-client, file-manager, json-formatter). Repeated invocations of skillfortify lock on the same configuration produce byte-identical output (verified in Experiment E6, Section 9.7).

  2. (2)

    Dependency resolution. The json-formatter skill declares a dependency on file-manager with constraint >=2.0.0. The resolver selected version 2.1.0, which satisfies the constraint.

  3. (3)

    Trust scores at lock time. Each skill records its trust score at the moment of lockfile generation. This enables temporal comparison: if a future skillfortify lock produces a lower trust score for the same skill version, it signals degraded confidence (e.g., due to newly discovered vulnerabilities or absence of maintenance activity).

  4. (4)

    Analysis status. The api-client skill has a "warning" status with one low-severity finding. This does not prevent lockfile generation (only "critical" status blocks locking by default) but is recorded for audit purposes.

  5. (5)

    Integrity hash. The top-level integrity field is a SHA-256 hash of the canonical JSON serialization of the entire skills object. Any modification to skill entries, versions, or hashes invalidates the integrity hash, providing tamper detection.

Canonical serialization.

Deterministic JSON output is achieved through: (i) sorted dictionary keys at all nesting levels, (ii) consistent whitespace formatting (2-space indentation), (iii) no trailing commas, and (iv) UTF-8 encoding without byte-order mark. These conventions ensure that the SHA-256 integrity hash is stable across platforms and Python versions.
